chapters.title: Chapter 1. In which Phileas Fogg and Passepartout Accept each Other, the One as Master, the Other as Man
paragraphs: Mr. Phileas Fogg boede i 1872 i nummer 7 Saville Row, Burlington Gardens — huset hvor Sheridan døde i 1814. Han var et af de mest iøjnefaldende medlemmer af Reform Club, selvom han syntes at gøre alt, hvad han kunne, for at undgå at tiltrække opmærksomhed: en gådefuld skikkelse, om hvem man kun vidste lidt, ud over at han var en dannet verdensmand. Folk sagde, at han lignede Byron — i det mindste var hans hoved Byronsk; men han var en skægget, fredsommelig Byron, den slags, der kunne leve tusind år uden at ælde.

En englænder, ganske bestemt. Om han var londoner, var mindre klart. Han blev aldrig set på børsen, ej heller i banken eller i kontorerne i »City«; ingen skibe lagde til i Londons havne, som han ejede; han beklædte intet offentligt embede; han havde aldrig været indskrevet ved nogen af Inns of Court — hverken Temple, Lincoln's Inn eller Gray's Inn — og hans stemme havde aldrig lydt i Court of Chancery, Exchequer, Queen's Bench eller de kirkelige domstole. Han var med sikkerhed ingen fabrikant, ingen købmand, ingen godsejer. Hans navn var ukendt i de videnskabelige og lærde selskaber, og han var aldrig blevet set deltage i forhandlinger ved Royal Institution, London Institution, Artisan's Association eller Institution of Arts and Sciences. Han tilhørte kort sagt ingen af de utallige selskaber, der vrimler i den engelske hovedstad, fra de harmoniske til entomologernes, hvis hovedformål er at udrydde skadelige insekter.
Phileas Fogg var medlem af Reform Club, og det var det hele.
Hvordan han havde båret sig ad med at få adgang til denne eksklusive klub, var enkelt nok.
Han var blevet anbefalet af Baring-bankhuset, hvor han havde en åben kreditlinje. Hans checks blev altid betalt prompte fra hans konto, som altid var velforsynet.

Var Phileas Fogg rig? Uden tvivl. Men hvordan han havde tjent sin formue, kunne selv de, der kendte ham bedst, ikke gætte sig til, og Mr. Fogg selv var den sidste, man ville stille spørgsmålet til. Han var ikke ødsel, men heller ikke nærig; hver gang han hørte, at der var brug for penge til et ædelt, nyttigt eller velgørende formål, leverede han dem stille, undertiden anonymt. Han var kort sagt den mindst meddelsomme af mænd. Han talte meget lidt og virkede så meget mere gådefuld på grund af sin tavse facon. Hans daglige vaner var fuldt synlige, men alt, hvad han gjorde, var så nøjagtigt det samme, som han altid havde gjort før, at de nysgerriges skarpsindighed blev grundigt slået ud af kurs.

Havde han rejst? Det syntes sandsynligt, for ingen lod til at kende verden mere fortroligt. Der fandtes intet sted så fjernt, at han ikke virkede på fortrolig fod med det. Han korrigerede ofte, med få klare ord, de tusind gisninger, klubmedlemmerne fremsatte om forsvundne eller ukendte rejsende, idet han pegede på de sande sandsynligheder og syntes begavet med en slags klarsyn, så ofte bekræftede begivenhederne hans forudsigelser. Han måtte have rejst overalt, i det mindste i ånden.

Hvad der i hvert fald var sikkert, var, at Phileas Fogg ikke havde forladt London i mange år. De, der kendte ham bedre end de andre, erklærede, at ingen kunne påstå at have set ham noget andet sted. Hans eneste tidsfordriv var at læse aviser og spille whist. Han vandt ofte ved dette spil, der — som et tavst spil — harmonerede med hans natur; men hans gevinster gik aldrig i hans pung, men blev sat til side som en fond til hans velgørenhedsformål. Mr. Fogg spillede ikke for at vinde, men for spillets skyld. Spillet var i hans øjne en kappestrid, en kamp mod en vanskelighed, men en ubevægelig, utrættelig kamp, der passede til hans smag.

Phileas Fogg vidste man ikke at have hverken kone eller børn, hvilket kan ske for de hæderligste af mænd; eller slægtninge eller nære venner, hvilket bestemt er mere usædvanligt. Han boede alene i sit hus i Saville Row, hvor ingen nogensinde trængte ind. En enkelt tjener var nok til at passe ham. Han spiste morgenmad og middag i klubben på matematisk fastsatte tidspunkter, i samme rum, ved samme bord, uden nogensinde at indtage sine måltider sammen med de andre medlemmer, endsige medbringe en gæst; og han gik hjem præcis ved midnat, blot for straks at gå i seng. Han brugte aldrig de hyggelige værelser, som Reform stiller til rådighed for sine begunstigede medlemmer. Han tilbragte ti af døgnets fireogtyve timer i Saville Row, enten sovende eller med sin morgentoilette. Når han valgte at gå en tur, var det altid med regelmæssige skridt i indgangshallen med dens mosaikgulv, eller i den runde galleri med kuplen båret af tyve røde porfyr-ioniske søjler og oplyst af blåmalede vinduer. Når han spiste morgenmad eller middag, samvirkede alle klubbens ressourcer — dens køkkener og spiskamre, dens smørrum og mejeri — om at fylde hans bord med den fineste kost; han blev serveret af de mest alvorlige tjenere, i jakkesæt og sko med svaneskindssåler, der bød retterne frem på særligt porcelæn og det fineste linned; klubbens karafler, fra en støbeform der forlængst er gået tabt, indeholdt hans sherry, hans portvin og hans kanelkrydrede claret; mens hans drikkevarer blev kølet med is, der var bragt for store omkostninger fra de amerikanske søer.
Hvis det at leve på denne måde er at være excentrisk, så må det indrømmes, at der er noget godt ved excentricitet.

Villaen i Saville Row var, skønt ikke overdådig, særdeles komfortabel. Beboerens vaner krævede kun lidt af den ene tjener, men Phileas Fogg forlangte, at han skulle være næsten overmenneskeligt prompte og regelmæssig. På selve denne 2. oktober havde han afskediget James Forster, fordi den uheldige yngling havde bragt ham barbervand på fireogfirs grader Fahrenheit i stedet for seksogfirs; og han ventede nu på sin efterfølger, der skulle ankomme til huset mellem elleve og halv tolv.

Phileas Fogg sad lige op i sin lænestol, med fødderne tæt sammen som en grenader på parade, hænderne hvilende på knæene, kroppen rank, hovedet løftet; han betragtede stadigt et kompliceret ur, som viste timer, minutter, sekunder, dage, måneder og år. Præcis klokken halv tolv ville Mr. Fogg, som han gjorde hver dag, forlade Saville Row og gå til Reform.
I dette øjeblik lød et bank på døren til den hyggelige lejlighed, hvor Phileas Fogg sad, og James Forster, den afskedigede tjener, viste sig.
»Den nye tjener,« sagde han.
En ung mand på tredive trådte frem og bukkede.
»De er franskmand, mener jeg,« spurgte Phileas Fogg, »og Deres navn er John?«

»Jean, hvis monsieur tillader,« svarede den nyankomne, »Jean Passepartout — et tilnavn, der har hængt ved mig, fordi jeg har et naturligt talent for at smutte ud af én beskæftigelse og ind i en anden. Jeg tror, jeg er ærlig, monsieur, men for at tale rent ud, har jeg haft adskillige fag. Jeg har været omvandrende sanger, cirkusrytter, der plejede at springe som Leotard og danse på line som Blondin. Så blev jeg gymnastiklærer for at gøre bedre brug af mine evner; og derefter var jeg sergent i brandvæsenet i Paris og hjalp ved mange store brande. Men jeg forlod Frankrig for fem år siden, og da jeg ville smage huslivets sødme, tog jeg tjeneste som kammertjener her i England. Da jeg fandt mig selv uden plads og hørte, at Monsieur Phileas Fogg var den mest nøjagtige og rolige gentleman i Det Forenede Kongerige, er jeg kommet til monsieur i håbet om at leve et stille liv hos ham og endda at glemme navnet Passepartout.«
»Passepartout passer mig,« svarede Mr. Fogg. »De er velanbefalet; jeg har hørt godt om Dem. De kender mine betingelser?«
»Ja, monsieur.«
»Godt. Hvad er klokken?«
»Toogtyve minutter over elleve,« svarede Passepartout og trak et enormt sølvur op fra lommens dybder.
»De går for langsomt,« sagde Mr. Fogg.
»Tilgiv mig, monsieur — det er umuligt —«
»De går fire minutter for langsomt. Det er lige meget; det er nok at notere fejlen. Fra dette øjeblik, niogtyve minutter over elleve, formiddag, onsdag den 2. oktober, er De i min tjeneste.«
Phileas Fogg rejste sig, tog sin hat i venstre hånd, satte den på hovedet med en automatisk bevægelse og gik uden et ord.

Passepartout hørte gadedøren smække i én gang; det var hans nye herre, der gik ud. Han hørte den smække igen; det var hans forgænger, James Forster, der nu også gik. Passepartout var alene tilbage i huset i Saville Row.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. In which Passepartout is Convinced that He Has at Last Found His Ideal
paragraphs: »Sandelig,« mumlede Passepartout en smule forfjamsket, »jeg har set folk hos Madame Tussaud, der var lige så livlige som min nye herre!«
Madame Tussauds »folk« er, det skal bemærkes, lavet af voks, og de har mange besøgende i London; kun talen mangler for at gøre dem menneskelige.

Under sit korte møde med Mr. Fogg havde Passepartout omhyggeligt iagttaget sin nye herre. Han syntes at være en mand på omkring fyrre, med fine, smukke træk og en høj, velbygget skikkelse; hans hår og bakkenbarter var lyse, hans pande glat og uden rynker, hans ansigt ret blegt, hans tænder strålende. Hans åsyn besad i højeste grad, hvad fysiognomister kalder »ro i handling«, den kvalitet, der kendetegner dem, der handler frem for at tale. Rolig og flegmatisk, med et klart blik, virkede Mr. Fogg som et fuldendt eksemplar af den engelske fatning, som Angelica Kauffmann har gengivet så dygtigt på lærred. Set i sit daglige livs forskellige faser gav han indtrykket af at være fuldkomment afbalanceret, lige så nøjagtigt indstillet som et Leroy-kronometer. Phileas Fogg var ganske rigtigt nøjagtigheden i egen person, og denne egenskab viste sig endda i udtrykket af hans hænder og fødder; for hos mennesker, som hos dyr, udtrykker selve lemmerne lidenskaberne.

Han var så nøjagtig, at han aldrig havde travlt, var altid parat, og var økonomisk med både sine skridt og sine bevægelser. Han tog aldrig ét skridt for meget og nåede altid sit mål ad den korteste vej; han gjorde ingen overflødige gestus og blev aldrig set rørt eller ophidset. Han var den mest velovervejede mand i verden, og dog ankom han altid i det præcise øjeblik.
Han levede alene og så at sige uden for ethvert socialt forhold; og da han vidste, at man i denne verden må regne med friktion, og at friktion forsinker, gned han sig aldrig op ad nogen.

Hvad angik Passepartout, var han en ægte pariser af Paris. Siden han havde forladt sit eget land for at tage tjeneste som kammertjener i England, havde han forgæves søgt efter en herre efter sit hjerte. Passepartout var på ingen måde en af de næbbede dumrianer, som Molière skildrer, med et frækt blik og næsen i sky; han var en hæderlig fyr med et behageligt ansigt, læberne en smule fremstående, blid af facon og imødekommende, med et godt rundt hoved af den slags, man gerne ser på en vens skuldre. Hans øjne var blå, hans teint rødmosset, hans skikkelse næsten kraftig og velbygget, hans krop muskuløs, og hans fysiske kræfter fuldt udviklede gennem ungdomsårenes øvelser. Hans brune hår var noget pjusket; for skønt de antikke billedhuggere siges at have kendt atten metoder til at arrangere Minervas lokker, kendte Passepartout kun én til at ordne sit eget: tre strøg med en grovtandet kam fuldendte hans toilette.

Det ville være dumdristigt at forudsige, hvordan Passepartouts livlige natur ville stemme overens med Mr. Fogg. Det var umuligt at sige, om den nye tjener ville vise sig at være så absolut metodisk, som hans herre krævede; kun erfaringen kunne afgøre spørgsmålet. Passepartout havde i sine unge år været noget af en omflakkende sjæl og længtes nu efter ro; men hidtil havde han ikke fundet den, skønt han allerede havde tjent i ti engelske huse. Han kunne ikke slå rod i nogen af dem; til hans store ærgrelse var hans herrer uden undtagelse luneagtige og uregelmæssige, evigt på farten rundt i landet eller på udkig efter eventyr. Hans sidste herre, unge Lord Longferry, medlem af Parlamentet, blev efter at have tilbragt nætterne på værtshusene i Haymarket alt for ofte bragt hjem om morgenen på politibetjentes skuldre. Passepartout, der ønskede at respektere den gentleman, han tjente, vovede en mild bebrejdelse over sådan opførsel; den blev dårligt modtaget, og han tog sin afsked. Da han hørte, at Mr. Phileas Fogg søgte en tjener, og at hans liv var én ubrudt regelmæssighed — at han hverken rejste eller overnattede uden for hjemmet — følte han sig sikker på, at dette var den plads, han havde søgt. Han meldte sig og blev antaget, som vi har set.

Klokken halv tolv befandt Passepartout sig altså alene i huset i Saville Row. Han begyndte sin inspektion uden tøven og gennemsøgte det fra kælder til kvist. Et så rent, så velordnet, så højtideligt hus behagede ham; det forekom ham som en sneglehus, oplyst og opvarmet med gas, hvilket tjente begge formål. Da Passepartout nåede til anden sal, genkendte han straks det værelse, han skulle bo i, og var godt tilfreds med det. Elektriske klokker og taleslanger sørgede for forbindelsen til de nedre etager; mens der på kaminhylden stod et elektrisk ur, præcis magen til det i Mr. Foggs soveværelse, og begge slog det samme sekund i samme øjeblik. »Det er godt, det dur,« sagde Passepartout til sig selv.

Så bemærkede han, ophængt over uret, et kort, der ved nærmere eftersyn viste sig at være et program over husets daglige rutine. Det omfattede alt, der krævedes af tjeneren, fra otte om morgenen — det præcise tidspunkt, hvor Phileas Fogg stod op — indtil halv tolv, hvor han gik til Reform Club: alle tjenestens detaljer, te og toast treogtyve minutter over otte, barbervand syvogtredive minutter over ni, morgentoilette tyve minutter i ti. Alt fra halv tolv formiddag indtil midnat, hvor den metodiske gentleman gik til ro, var reguleret og forudset.

Mr. Foggs garderobe var rigeligt forsynet og af den bedste smag. Hvert par bukser, hver jakke og vest bar et nummer, der angav årstid og sæson, hvor det skulle lægges frem til brug; og samme system blev anvendt på herrens sko. Kort sagt var huset i Saville Row — som under den berømte, men ødsle Sheridan må have været et sandt tempel for uorden og uro — hyggeligheden, komforten og metoden idealiseret. Der var intet arbejdsværelse og ingen bøger, hvilket ville have været ganske unyttigt for Mr. Fogg; for i Reform stod to biblioteker, det ene med almen litteratur, det andet med jura og politik, til hans rådighed. Et pengeskab af moderat størrelse stod i hans soveværelse, bygget til at trodse både ild og indbrudstyve; men Passepartout fandt ingen våben nogetsteds, intet jagtudstyr; alt vidnede om de mest fredelige og stilfærdige vaner.

Efter at have gransket huset fra øverst til nederst gned han sig i hænderne, et bredt smil bredte sig over hans træk, og han sagde glædestrålende: »Det er præcis det, jeg ville have! Ah, vi skal nok komme overens, Mr. Fogg og jeg! Hvilken huslig og regelmæssig gentleman! En rigtig maskine — nuvel, jeg har intet imod at tjene en maskine.«

chapters.title: Chapter 3. In which a Conversation Takes Place which Seems Likely to Cost Phileas Fogg Dear
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg lukkede døren til sit hus klokken halv tolv, satte sin højre fod foran den venstre fem hundrede femoghalvfjerds gange og sin venstre fod foran den højre fem hundrede seksoghalvfjerds gange, og nåede Reform Club — en imponerende bygning i Pall Mall, der ikke kan have kostet mindre end tre millioner. Han gik direkte til spisesalen, hvis ni vinduer åbner mod en smagfuld have, hvor træerne allerede var forgyldte med efterårsfarver, og indtog sin plads ved sit sædvanlige bord, kuverten allerede dækket. Hans morgenmad bestod af en mellemret, en grillet fisk med Reading-sovs, en skarlagensrød skive roastbeef garneret med svampe, en rabarber- og stikkelsbærtærte og en mundfuld Cheshire-ost, alt skyllet ned med adskillige kopper te, som Reform er berømt for. Han rejste sig tretten minutter i et og begav sig til den store hal, et overdådigt rum med prægtigt indrammede malerier. En lakaj rakte ham en uskåret _Times_, som han gik i gang med at skære op med en lang fortroligheds dygtighed. Læsningen af denne avis optog Phileas Fogg indtil kvart i fire, mens _Standard_, hans næste opgave, optog ham indtil middagstid. Middagen forløb som morgenmaden, og Mr. Fogg dukkede atter op i læsesalen og satte sig med _Pall Mall_ tyve minutter i seks. En halv time senere kom flere medlemmer af Reform ind og trak op til kaminen, hvor en kulild brændte støt. Det var Mr. Foggs sædvanlige whist-makkere: Andrew Stuart, ingeniør; John Sullivan og Samuel Fallentin, bankmænd; Thomas Flanagan, brygger; og Gauthier Ralph, en af direktørerne for Bank of England — alle velhavende og højt respekterede mænd, selv i en klub, der omfattede den engelske handels og finans' fyrster.
»Nå, Ralph,« sagde Thomas Flanagan, »hvad med det røveri?«
»Åh,« svarede Stuart, »Banken kommer til at miste pengene.«

»Tværtimod,« afbrød Ralph, »jeg håber, vi endnu kan få fat i tyven. Dygtige detektiver er sendt til alle vigtige havne i Amerika og på kontinentet, og han skal være en kløgtig fyr, hvis han slipper gennem deres fingre.«
»Men har I et signalement af tyven?« spurgte Stuart.
»For det første er han slet ikke nogen tyv,« svarede Ralph bestemt.
»Hvad! En fyr, der stikker af med femoghalvtreds tusind pund, ingen tyv?«
»Nej.«
»Så er han måske fabrikant.«
»_Daily Telegraph_ siger, han er en gentleman.«

Det var Phileas Fogg, hvis hoved nu kom til syne bag aviserne, der kom med denne bemærkning. Han hilste på sine venner og blandede sig i samtalen. Sagen, der dannede dens emne, og som hele byen talte om, var indtruffet tre dage tidligere i Bank of England. En pakke pengesedler til en værdi af femoghalvtreds tusind pund var blevet taget fra hovedkassererens bord, mens denne embedsmand i det øjeblik var optaget af at registrere modtagelsen af tre shillings og seks pence. Naturligvis kunne han ikke have øjnene alle steder. Det skal bemærkes, at Bank of England nærer en rørende tillid til offentlighedens ærlighed. Der er hverken vagter eller gitre til at beskytte dens skatte; guld, sølv, pengesedler ligger frit fremme, prisgivet den første den bedste. En skarp iagttager af engelske skikke fortæller, at han en dag, da han befandt sig i et af bankens rum, fik den nysgerrighed at undersøge en guldbarre på syv eller otte pund. Han tog den op, gransked den, rakte den videre til sin nabo, der rakte den videre til den næste mand, og så videre, indtil barren, der gik fra hånd til hånd, blev båret ned til enden af en mørk gang; den vendte ikke tilbage til sin plads i en halv time. I al den tid havde kassereren end ikke løftet hovedet. Men i nærværende tilfælde var tingene ikke gået så glat. Da pakken med sedler ikke kunne findes, da klokken fem slog på det tunge ur i »tegnestuen«, blev beløbet ført over på tabskontoen. Så snart røveriet blev opdaget, ilede udvalgte detektiver til Liverpool, Glasgow, Le Havre, Suez, Brindisi, New York og andre havne, ansporet af den udlovede dusør — to tusind pund og fem procent af det beløb, der måtte blive inddrevet. Detektiver fik også til opgave nøje at overvåge alle, der ankom til eller forlod London med tog, og en retslig undersøgelse blev straks indledt.

Der var virkelige grunde til at antage, som _Daily Telegraph_ skrev, at tyven ikke tilhørte nogen professionel bande. På dagen for røveriet havde en velklædt gentleman af dannet væsen, med velstillet udseende, været bemærket gående ud og ind i kassesalen, hvor forbrydelsen havde fundet sted. Et signalement af ham blev let opnået og bragt videre til detektiverne; og nogle håbefulde sjæle, hvoraf Ralph var en, opgav ikke håbet om at fange ham. Aviserne og klubberne var fulde af sagen, og overalt diskuterede folk udsigterne for en vellykket forfølgelse. Reform Club var særligt opstemt, idet flere af dens medlemmer var embedsmænd i banken.

Ralph ville ikke indrømme, at detektivernes arbejde sandsynligvis ville være forgæves; han mente, at den udlovede præmie ville stimulere deres iver og aktivitet betydeligt. Men Stuart delte langtfra denne tillid; og da de tog plads ved whist-bordet, fortsatte de med at diskutere sagen. Stuart og Flanagan spillede sammen, mens Phileas Fogg havde Fallentin som makker. Mens spillet skred frem, ophørte samtalen, undtagen mellem hænderne, hvor den blussede op igen.
»Jeg fastholder,« sagde Stuart, »at chancerne er på tyvens side, der må være en snu fyr.«
»Nuvel, men hvor kan han flygte hen?« spurgte Ralph. »Intet land er sikkert for ham.«
»Pyt!«
»Hvor skulle han så kunne tage hen?«
»Åh, det ved jeg ikke. Verden er stor nok.«
»Det var den engang,« sagde Phileas Fogg med dæmpet stemme. »Skær, hr.,« tilføjede han og rakte kortene til Thomas Flanagan.
Diskussionen døde hen under denne hånd; bagefter tog Stuart tråden op igen.
»Hvad mener De med 'engang'? Er verden blevet mindre?«

»Bestemt,« svarede Ralph. »Jeg er enig med Mr. Fogg. Verden er blevet mindre, eftersom en mand nu kan komme verden rundt ti gange hurtigere end for hundrede år siden. Og det er grunden til, at jagten på denne tyv har større sandsynlighed for at lykkes.«
»Og også grunden til, at tyven kan slippe væk lettere.«
»Vær så venlig at spille, Mr. Stuart,« sagde Phileas Fogg.

Men den skeptiske Stuart var ikke overbevist, og da hånden var spillet, sagde han ivrigt: »De har en mærkelig måde, Ralph, at bevise på, at verden er blevet mindre. Så fordi man kan komme verden rundt på tre måneder —«
»På firs dage,« afbrød Phileas Fogg.

»Det er sandt, mine herrer,« tilføjede John Sullivan. »Kun firs dage, nu hvor strækningen mellem Rothal og Allahabad på Great Indian Peninsula Railway er åbnet. Her er beregningen lavet af _Daily Telegraph_:—

Fra London til Suez _via_ Mont Cenis og Brindisi, med tog og dampskib ................. 7 dage Fra Suez til Bombay, med damper .................... 13 » Fra Bombay til Calcutta, med tog ................... 3 » Fra Calcutta til Hong Kong, med damper ............. 13 » Fra Hong Kong til Yokohama (Japan), med damper ..... 6 » Fra Yokohama til San Francisco, med damper ......... 22 » Fra San Francisco til New York, med tog ............. 7 » Fra New York til London, med damper og tog ........ 9 » ------- I alt ............................................ 80 dage.«
»Ja, på firs dage!« udbrød Stuart, der i sin ophidselse lavede en fejlgivning. »Men det tager ikke højde for dårligt vejr, modvind, skibsforlis, jernbaneuheld og så videre.«
»Alt inklusive,« svarede Phileas Fogg og fortsatte med at spille på trods af diskussionen.
»Men sæt at hinduerne eller indianerne river skinnerne op,« sagde Stuart; »sæt at de standser togene, plyndrer bagagevognene og skalperer passagererne!«
»Alt inklusive,« replicerede Fogg roligt og tilføjede, idet han kastede sine kort: »To trumfer.«
Stuart, som det var hans tur at give, samlede dem op og fortsatte: »De har ret, Mr. Fogg, teoretisk, men i praksis —«
»Også i praksis, Mr. Stuart.«
»Jeg ville gerne se Dem gøre det på firs dage.«
»Det afhænger af Dem. Skal vi tage afsted?«
»Himlen bevare mig! Men jeg ville vædde fire tusind pund på, at en sådan rejse, foretaget under disse betingelser, er umulig.«
»Tværtimod ganske mulig,« svarede Mr. Fogg.
»Nuvel, gør det da!«
»Rejsen rundt om jorden på firs dage?«
»Ja.«
»Jeg ville intet hellere.«
»Hvornår?«
»Straks. Kun advarer jeg Dem om, at jeg vil gøre det på Deres bekostning.«
»Det er absurd!« råbte Stuart, der var begyndt at ærgre sig over sin vens stædighed. »Kom, lad os komme videre med spillet.«
»Giv da igen,« sagde Phileas Fogg. »Der er en fejlgivning.«
Stuart tog kortbunken op med en feberhed hånd; så satte han den pludselig fra sig igen.
»Nuvel, Mr. Fogg,« sagde han, »så lad det være: jeg vædder fire tusinde pund på det.«
»Tag det roligt, min kære Stuart,« sagde Fallentin. »Det er kun en spøg.«
»Når jeg siger, at jeg vil vædde,« svarede Stuart, »så mener jeg det.«
»Udmærket,« sagde Mr. Fogg; og idet han vendte sig mod de andre, fortsatte han: »Jeg har et indskud på tyve tusind hos Barings, som jeg gerne vil sætte på spil.«
»Tyve tusind pund!« udbrød Sullivan. »Tyve tusind pund, som De kunne miste ved en enkelt tilfældig forsinkelse!«
»Det uforudsete findes ikke,« svarede Phileas Fogg roligt.
»Men, Mr. Fogg, firs dage er kun beregningen af den mindst mulige tid, hvorpå rejsen kan gennemføres.«
»Et velbenyttet minimum er nok til alt.«
»Men for ikke at overskride det må De springe matematisk fra togene til damperne og fra damperne tilbage på togene.«
»Jeg vil springe — matematisk.«
»De spøger.«

»En ægte englænder spøger ikke, når han taler om så alvorlig en ting som et væddemål,« svarede Phileas Fogg højtideligt. »Jeg vædder tyve tusind pund mod enhver, der måtte ønske det, på at jeg vil foretage rejsen rundt om jorden på firs dage eller mindre; på nitten hundrede og tyve timer, eller hundrede og femten tusind to hundrede minutter. Tager De imod?«
»Vi tager imod,« svarede Messrs. Stuart, Fallentin, Sullivan, Flanagan og Ralph, efter at have rådført sig med hinanden.
»Godt,« sagde Mr. Fogg. »Toget afgår til Dover kvart i ni. Jeg tager det.«
»I aften?« spurgte Stuart.

»I aften,« svarede Phileas Fogg. Han tog en lommealmanak op og slog efter, hvorefter han tilføjede: »Da i dag er onsdag den 2. oktober, skal jeg være tilbage i London, i netop dette rum af Reform Club, lørdag den 21. december klokken kvart i ni om aftenen; ellers vil de tyve tusind pund, der nu står deponeret i mit navn hos Barings, tilhøre Dem, faktisk og retligt, mine herrer. Her er en check på beløbet.«

Et memorandum om væddemålet blev straks udfærdiget og underskrevet af alle seks parter, mens Phileas Fogg bevarede en stoisk fatning. Han væddede bestemt ikke for at vinde og havde kun sat de tyve tusind pund — halvdelen af sin formue — fordi han forudså, at han måtte bruge den anden halvdel til at gennemføre dette vanskelige, for ikke at sige umulige projekt. Hans modstandere virkede for deres part stærkt urolige; ikke så meget på grund af værdien af deres indsats, som fordi de havde visse skrupler ved at vædde på vilkår, der var så ufordelagtige for deres ven.
Klokken slog syv, og selskabet tilbød at afbryde spillet, så Mr. Fogg kunne gøre sig klar til afrejsen.
»Jeg er helt klar nu,« lød hans rolige svar. »Ruder er trumf: vær så gode at spille, mine herrer.«

chapters.title: Chapter 4. In which Phileas Fogg Astounds Passepartout, His Servant
paragraphs: Efter at have vundet tyve guinea i whist og taget afsked med sine venner forlod Phileas Fogg Reform Club fem og tyve minutter over syv.

Passepartout, der samvittighedsfuldt havde studeret programmet for sine pligter, blev mere end overrasket over at se sin herre begå den unøjagtighed at vise sig på dette uvante tidspunkt; for ifølge reglen skulle han først være i Saville Row ved nøjagtigt midnat.
Mr. Fogg gik op til sit soveværelse og kaldte: »Passepartout!«
Passepartout svarede ikke. Det kunne ikke være ham, der blev kaldt; det var ikke det rette tidspunkt.
»Passepartout!« gentog Mr. Fogg uden at hæve stemmen.
Passepartout viste sig.
»Jeg har kaldt på Dem to gange,« bemærkede hans herre.
»Men det er ikke midnat,« svarede den anden og viste sit ur.
»Det ved jeg; jeg bebrejder Dem intet. Vi tager til Dover og Calais om ti minutter.«
Et forundret grin bredte sig over Passepartouts runde ansigt; tydeligvis havde han ikke fattet, hvad hans herre mente.
»Monsieur vil rejse hjemmefra?«
»Ja,« svarede Phileas Fogg. »Vi skal rundt om jorden.«
Passepartout spilede øjnene op, løftede øjenbrynene, holdt hænderne op og syntes nær ved at segne, så overvældet var han af forbløffet forbavselse.
»Rundt om jorden!« mumlede han.
»På firs dage,« svarede Mr. Fogg. »Så vi har ikke et øjeblik at miste.«
»Men kufferterne?« hivede Passepartout efter vejret, mens han ubevidst rokkede med hovedet fra side til side.

»Vi tager ingen kufferter med; kun en rejsetaske, med to skjorter og tre par strømper til mig, og det samme til Dem. Vi køber vores tøj undervejs. Hent min regnfrakke og rejsekappe ned, og et par solide sko, skønt vi næppe får meget at gå. Skynd Dem!«
Passepartout forsøgte at svare, men kunne ikke. Han gik ud, kravlede op til sit eget værelse, sank ned i en stol og mumlede: »Det er da skønt! Og jeg, som ville have ro!«

Mekanisk gik han i gang med forberedelserne til afrejsen. Rundt om jorden på firs dage! Var hans herre en tåbe? Nej. Var det en spøg, da? De skulle til Dover; godt! Til Calais; også godt! Når alt kom til alt, ville Passepartout, der havde været væk fra Frankrig i fem år, ikke være ked af at sætte foden på sit fædreland igen. Måske ville de komme helt til Paris, og det ville være godt for hans øjne at se Paris igen. Men ganske vist ville en gentleman, der var så sparsommelig med sine skridt, gøre holdt der — uden tvivl; og dog var det ikke desto mindre sandt, at han rejste bort, denne mest huslige af mænd!

Klokken otte havde Passepartout pakket den beskedne rejsetaske, der rummede både hans herres og hans egen garderobe; så lukkede han, stadig urolig i sindet, omhyggeligt døren til sit værelse og gik ned til Mr. Fogg.

Mr. Fogg var helt klar. Under armen sås et rødbundet eksemplar af Bradshaw's Continental Railway Steam Transit and General Guide, med dens fartplaner over damperes og jernbaners ankomst og afgang. Han tog rejsetasken, åbnede den og lod en pæn rulle Bank of England-sedler glide ned i den, sedler der ville gå overalt, hvor han måtte komme.
»De har ikke glemt noget?« spurgte han.
»Intet, monsieur.«
»Min regnfrakke og kappe?«
»Her er de.«
»Godt. Tag denne rejsetaske,« sagde han og rakte den til Passepartout. »Pas godt på den, for der er tyve tusind pund i den.«
Passepartout var lige ved at tabe tasken, som om de tyve tusind pund havde været i guld og tyngede ham ned.

Herre og tjener gik så ned, gadedøren blev dobbeltlåst, og for enden af Saville Row tog de en droske og kørte hurtigt til Charing Cross. Drosken stoppede ved jernbanestationen tyve minutter over otte. Passepartout sprang ned fra bukken og fulgte sin herre, der, efter at have betalt kuskens og var ved at gå ind på stationen, da en stakkels tiggerske med et barn i armene, hendes bare fødder smurt med mudder, hendes hoved dækket af en sølle kyse, hvorfra hang en flosset fjer, og hendes skuldre svøbt i et pjaltet sjal, nærmede sig og bedrøvet bad om almisser.
Mr. Fogg trak de tyve guinea op, som han netop havde vundet i whist, og rakte dem til tiggerne, idet han sagde: »Værsgo, min gode kone. Jeg er glad for, at jeg mødte Dem«; og gik videre.
Passepartout følte en fugtig fornemmelse om øjnene; hans herres handling havde rørt hans modtagelige hjerte.
Da to førsteklasses billetter til Paris var blevet hurtigt købt, var Mr. Fogg på vej over stationen mod toget, da han fik øje på sine fem venner fra Reform.
»Nuvel, mine herrer,« sagde han, »jeg er på vej, som De ser; og hvis De vil undersøge mit pas, når jeg kommer tilbage, vil De kunne bedømme, om jeg har gennemført den aftalte rejse.«
»Åh, det ville være ganske unødvendigt, Mr. Fogg,« sagde Ralph høfligt. »Vi vil stole på Deres ord som æresmand.«
»De glemmer ikke, hvornår De skal være tilbage i London?« spurgte Stuart.
»Om firs dage; lørdag den 21. december 1872 klokken kvart i ni om aftenen. Farvel, mine herrer.«
Phileas Fogg og hans tjener tog plads i en førsteklasses kupé tyve minutter i ni; fem minutter senere hvinede fløjten, og toget gled langsomt ud af stationen.

Natten var mørk, og en fin, vedholdende regn faldt. Phileas Fogg, lunt placeret i sit hjørne, åbnede ikke munden. Passepartout, der endnu ikke var kommet sig over sin forbløffelse, klyngede sig mekanisk til rejsetasken med dens enorme skat.
Netop som toget susede gennem Sydenham, udstødte Passepartout pludselig et fortvivlet skrig.
»Hvad er der i vejen?« spurgte Mr. Fogg.
»Ak! I min hast — jeg — jeg glemte —«
»Hvad?«
»At slukke gassen på mit værelse!«
»Ganske vist, unge mand,« svarede Mr. Fogg køligt; »den vil brænde — på Deres bekostning.«

chapters.title: Chapter 5. In which a New Species of Funds, Unknown to the Moneyed Men, Appears on ’change
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg rightly suspected that his departure from London would create a lively sensation at the West End. The news of the bet spread through the Reform Club and gave its members an exciting topic of conversation. From the club it soon got into the papers throughout England. The boasted “tour of the world” was talked about, disputed, argued over with as much warmth as if the subject were another Alabama claim. Some took the side of Phileas Fogg, but the great majority shook their heads and declared against him; it was absurd, impossible, they said, that the tour of the world could be made, except theoretically and on paper, in this minimum of time, and with the existing means of travel. The _Times, Standard, Morning Post_, and _Daily News_, and twenty other highly respectable newspapers dismissed Mr. Fogg’s project as madness; the _Daily Telegraph_ alone hesitantly supported him. People generally thought him a lunatic, and blamed his Reform Club friends for having accepted a wager that betrayed the mental aberration of its proposer.

Articles no less passionate than logical appeared on the question, for geography is one of the pet subjects of the English; and the columns devoted to Phileas Fogg’s venture were eagerly devoured by all classes of readers. At first a few rash individuals, principally of the gentler sex, took up his cause, which became still more popular when the _Illustrated London News_ came out with his portrait, copied from a photograph in the Reform Club. A few readers of the _Daily Telegraph_ even dared to say, “Why not, after all? Stranger things have come to pass.”

At last a long article appeared, on the 7th of October, in the bulletin of the Royal Geographical Society, which treated the question from every angle and demonstrated the utter folly of the enterprise.

Everything, it said, was against the travellers, every obstacle imposed by both man and nature. A miraculous coincidence in the times of departure and arrival, which was impossible, was absolutely necessary to his success. He might, perhaps, count on the arrival of trains at the appointed hours in Europe, where the distances were relatively moderate; but when he reckoned on crossing India in three days, and the United States in seven, could he rely without misgiving on accomplishing his task? There were accidents to machinery, the risk of trains running off the line, collisions, bad weather, blocking by snow—were not all these against Phileas Fogg? Would he not find himself, when travelling by steamer in winter, at the mercy of the winds and fogs? Is it uncommon for the best ocean steamers to be two or three days behind time? But a single delay would be enough to fatally break the chain of communication; should Phileas Fogg once miss, even by an hour, a steamer, he would have to wait for the next, and that would irrevocably ruin his attempt.
This article caused a great deal of noise, and, being reprinted in all the papers, seriously depressed the supporters of the rash tourist.

Everybody knows that England is the world of betting men, who rank rather higher than mere gamblers; to bet is in the English temperament. Not only the members of the Reform but the general public made heavy wagers for or against Phileas Fogg, who was set down in the betting books as if he were a race-horse. Bonds were issued and appeared on ’Change; “Phileas Fogg bonds” were offered at par or at a premium, and a great business was done in them. But five days after the article in the bulletin of the Geographical Society appeared, the demand began to fall: “Phileas Fogg” declined. They were offered in packages, first of five, then of ten, until at last nobody would take less than twenty, fifty, a hundred!

Lord Albemarle, an elderly paralytic gentleman, was now the only advocate of Phileas Fogg left. This noble lord, fastened to his chair, would have given his fortune to be able to make the tour of the world, even if it took ten years; and he bet five thousand pounds on Phileas Fogg. When the folly, as well as the uselessness, of the adventure was pointed out to him, he contented himself with replying, “If the thing is feasible, the first to do it ought to be an Englishman.”

The Fogg party dwindled steadily, everybody was going against him, and the bets stood at a hundred and fifty to one and two hundred to one; and a week after his departure an incident occurred that deprived him of backers at any price.
The commissioner of police was sitting in his office at nine o’clock one evening when the following telegraphic dispatch was put into his hands:
_Suez to London._
ROWAN, COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, SCOTLAND YARD: I’ve found the bank robber, Phileas Fogg. Send without delay warrant of arrest to Bombay.
FIX, _Detective_.

The effect of this dispatch was instantaneous. The polished gentleman disappeared, replaced by the bank robber. His photograph, which hung with those of the other members at the Reform Club, was examined in detail, and it betrayed, feature by feature, the description of the robber that had been given to the police. The mysterious habits of Phileas Fogg were recalled; his solitary ways, his sudden departure; and it seemed clear that, in undertaking a tour round the world on the pretext of a wager, he had had no other end in view than to elude the detectives and throw them off his track.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. In which Fix, the Detective, Betrays a Very Natural Impatience
paragraphs: The circumstances under which this telegraphic dispatch about Phileas Fogg was sent were as follows:

The steamer “Mongolia,” belonging to the Peninsular and Oriental Company, built of iron, of two thousand eight hundred tons burden and five hundred horse-power, was due at eleven o’clock a.m. on Wednesday, the 9th of October, at Suez. The “Mongolia” plied regularly between Brindisi and Bombay _viâ_ the Suez Canal, and was one of the fastest steamers belonging to the company, always making more than ten knots an hour between Brindisi and Suez, and nine and a half between Suez and Bombay.

Two men were walking up and down the wharves, among the crowd of natives and strangers who were staying in this once-straggling village—now, thanks to the enterprise of M. Lesseps, a fast-growing town. One was the British consul at Suez, who, despite the prophecies of the English Government and the unfavourable predictions of Stephenson, was in the habit of watching, from his office window, English ships pass daily to and fro on the great canal, by which the old roundabout route from England to India by the Cape of Good Hope was shortened by at least a half. The other was a small, slight-built personage, with a nervous, intelligent face and bright eyes peering out from under eyebrows he was incessantly twitching. He was just now showing unmistakable signs of impatience, nervously pacing up and down, unable to stand still for a moment. This was Fix, one of the detectives sent out from England in search of the bank robber; it was his task to watch every passenger arriving at Suez closely, and to follow up anyone who seemed a suspicious character or resembled the description of the criminal he had received two days before from police headquarters in London. The detective was evidently inspired by the hope of obtaining the splendid reward that would be the prize of success, and he awaited, with an easily understandable feverish impatience, the arrival of the steamer “Mongolia.”
“So you say, consul,” he asked for the twentieth time, “that this steamer is never behind time?”

“No, Mr. Fix,” replied the consul. “She was signalled yesterday at Port Said, and the rest of the way is nothing to such a craft. I repeat that the ‘Mongolia’ has been ahead of the time required by the company’s regulations, and gained the prize awarded for excess of speed.”
“Does she come directly from Brindisi?”

“Directly from Brindisi; she takes on the Indian mails there, and she left there Saturday at five p.m. Have patience, Mr. Fix; she will not be late. But really, I don’t see how, from the description you have, you will be able to recognise your man, even if he is on board the ‘Mongolia.’”

“A man rather feels the presence of these fellows, consul, than recognises them. You must have a scent for them, and a scent is like a sixth sense that combines hearing, seeing, and smelling. I’ve arrested more than one of these gentlemen in my time, and if my thief is on board, I’ll answer for it; he won’t slip through my fingers.”
“I hope so, Mr. Fix, for it was a heavy robbery.”
“A magnificent robbery, consul; fifty-five thousand pounds! We don’t often have such windfalls. Burglars are becoming so contemptible these days! A fellow gets hanged for a handful of shillings!”

“Mr. Fix,” said the consul, “I like your way of talking, and I hope you’ll succeed; but I fear you’ll find it far from easy. Don’t you see, the description you have there bears a singular resemblance to an honest man?”

“Consul,” remarked the detective dogmatically, “great robbers always resemble honest folks. Fellows with rascally faces have only one course to take, and that’s to remain honest; otherwise they’d be arrested out of hand. The artistic thing is to unmask honest countenances; it’s no light task, I admit, but a real art.”
Mr. Fix was evidently not without his share of self-conceit.

Little by little the scene on the quay grew more animated; sailors of various nations, merchants, ship-brokers, porters, fellahs bustled to and fro as if the steamer were expected at any moment. The weather was clear and slightly chilly. The minarets of the town loomed above the houses in the pale rays of the sun. A jetty pier, some two thousand yards long, stretched out into the roadstead. A number of fishing-smacks and coasting boats, some still keeping the fantastic shape of ancient galleys, could be seen on the Red Sea.
As he made his way through the busy crowd, Fix scrutinised the passers-by, as was his habit, with a keen, rapid glance.
It was now half-past ten.
“The steamer doesn’t come!” he exclaimed, as the port clock struck.
“She can’t be far off now,” returned his companion.
“How long will she stop at Suez?”
“Four hours; long enough to take on coal. It is thirteen hundred and ten miles from Suez to Aden, at the other end of the Red Sea, and she has to take on a fresh coal supply.”
“And does she go from Suez directly to Bombay?”
“Without putting in anywhere.”

“Good,” said Fix. “If the robber is on board, he will no doubt get off at Suez, so as to reach the Dutch or French colonies in Asia by some other route. He ought to know that he would not be safe an hour in India, which is English soil.”
“Unless,” objected the consul, “he is exceptionally shrewd. An English criminal, you know, is always better concealed in London than anywhere else.”

This observation gave the detective food for thought, and meanwhile the consul went away to his office. Fix, left alone, was more impatient than ever, having a presentiment that the robber was on board the “Mongolia.” If he had indeed left London intending to reach the New World, he would naturally take the route _viâ_ India, which was less watched—and harder to watch—than the Atlantic. But Fix’s reflections were soon interrupted by a succession of sharp whistles, which announced the arrival of the “Mongolia.” The porters and fellahs rushed down the quay, and a dozen boats pushed off from the shore to go and meet the steamer. Soon her gigantic hull appeared, gliding between the banks, and eleven o’clock struck as she anchored in the roadstead. She brought an unusual number of passengers, some of whom remained on deck to scan the picturesque panorama of the town, while the greater part disembarked into the boats and landed on the quay.

Fix took up a position and carefully examined each face and figure that appeared. Presently one of the passengers, after vigorously pushing his way through the importunate crowd of porters, came up to him and politely asked if he could point out the English consulate, at the same time showing a passport which he wished to have _visaed_. Fix instinctively took the passport, and with a rapid glance read the description of its bearer. An involuntary motion of surprise nearly escaped him, for the description in the passport was identical with that of the bank robber he had received from Scotland Yard.
“Is this your passport?” he asked.
“No, it’s my master’s.”
“And your master is—”
“He stayed on board.”
“But he must come to the consul’s in person, so as to establish his identity.”
“Oh, is that necessary?”
“Quite indispensable.”
“And where is the consulate?”
“There, on the corner of the square,” said Fix, pointing to a house two hundred steps off.
“I’ll go and fetch my master, who won’t be much pleased, however, at being disturbed.”
The passenger bowed to Fix and returned to the steamer.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Which Once More Demonstrates the Uselessness of Passports as Aids to Detectives
paragraphs: The detective passed down the quay and made his way rapidly to the consul’s office, where he was at once admitted to the presence of that official.
“Consul,” he said, without preamble, “I have strong reasons to believe that my man is a passenger on the ‘Mongolia.’” And he related what had just passed concerning the passport.

“Well, Mr. Fix,” replied the consul, “I shall not be sorry to see the rascal’s face; but perhaps he won’t come here—that is, if he is the person you suppose him to be. A robber doesn’t much like to leave traces of his flight behind him; and besides, he is not obliged to have his passport countersigned.”
“If he is as shrewd as I think he is, consul, he will come.”
“To have his passport _visaed?_”
“Yes. Passports are only good for annoying honest folks and helping rogues in their flight. I assure you it will be quite the thing for him to do; but I hope you will not _visa_ the passport.”
“Why not? If the passport is genuine, I have no right to refuse.”
“Still, I must keep this man here until I can get a warrant to arrest him from London.”
“Ah, that’s your look-out. But I cannot—”

The consul did not finish his sentence, for as he spoke a knock was heard at the door, and two strangers entered, one of them the servant Fix had met on the quay. The other, his master, held out his passport with the request that the consul would do him the favour of _visaing_ it. The consul took the document and read it carefully, while Fix observed, or rather devoured, the stranger with his eyes from a corner of the room.
“You are Mr. Phileas Fogg?” said the consul, after reading the passport.
“I am.”
“And this man is your servant?”
“He is: a Frenchman, named Passepartout.”
“You are from London?”
“Yes.”
“And you are going—”
“To Bombay.”
“Very good, sir. You know that a _visa_ is useless, and that no passport is required?”
“I know it, sir,” replied Phileas Fogg; “but I wish to prove, by your _visa_, that I came by way of Suez.”
“Very well, sir.”
The consul proceeded to sign and date the passport, after which he added his official seal. Mr. Fogg paid the customary fee, bowed coldly, and went out, followed by his servant.
“Well?” the detective asked.
“Well, he looks and acts like a perfectly honest man,” replied the consul.
“Possibly; but that is not the question. Do you think, consul, that this phlegmatic gentleman resembles, feature by feature, the robber whose description I have received?”
“I grant that; but then, you know, all descriptions—”
“I’ll make certain of it,” interrupted Fix. “The servant seems to me less mysterious than the master; besides, he’s a Frenchman, and can’t help talking. Excuse me for a little while, consul.”
Fix set off in search of Passepartout.

Meanwhile Mr. Fogg, after leaving the consulate, went to the quay, gave some orders to Passepartout, then took a boat out to the “Mongolia” and went down to his cabin. He took up his notebook, which contained the following memoranda:
“Left London, Wednesday, October 2nd, at 8.45 p.m.
“Reached Paris, Thursday, October 3rd, at 7.20 a.m.
“Left Paris, Thursday, at 8.40 a.m.
“Reached Turin by Mont Cenis, Friday, October 4th, at 6.35 a.m.
“Left Turin, Friday, at 7.20 a.m.
“Arrived at Brindisi, Saturday, October 5th, at 4 p.m.
“Sailed on the ‘Mongolia,’ Saturday, at 5 p.m.
“Reached Suez, Wednesday, October 9th, at 11 a.m.
“Total hours spent, 158½; or, in days, six days and a half.”

These dates were entered in an itinerary divided into columns, indicating the month, the day of the month, and the day for the stipulated and actual arrivals at each principal point—Paris, Brindisi, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Singapore, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, and London—from the 2nd of October to the 21st of December; with a space for setting down the gain made or the loss suffered on arrival at each locality. This methodical record contained an account of everything needed, and Mr. Fogg always knew whether he was behind or ahead of his time. On this Friday, October 9th, he noted his arrival at Suez, and observed that he had as yet neither gained nor lost. He sat down quietly to breakfast in his cabin, never once thinking of inspecting the town, being one of those Englishmen who are accustomed to see foreign countries through the eyes of their servants.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. In which Passepartout Talks Rather More, Perhaps, than is Prudent
paragraphs: Fix soon rejoined Passepartout, who was lounging and looking about on the quay, as though he didn’t feel that he, at least, was obliged not to see anything.
“Well, my friend,” said the detective, coming up with him, “is your passport _visaed?_”
“Ah, it’s you, is it, monsieur?” responded Passepartout. “Thanks, yes, the passport is all right.”
“And you are looking about you?”
“Yes; but we travel so fast that I seem to be journeying in a dream. So this is Suez?”
“Yes.”
“In Egypt?”
“Certainly, in Egypt.”
“And in Africa?”
“In Africa.”

“In Africa!” repeated Passepartout. “Just think, monsieur, I had no idea we should go farther than Paris; and all I saw of Paris was between twenty minutes past seven and twenty minutes before nine in the morning, between the Northern and Lyons stations, through the windows of a railway carriage, and in a driving rain! How I regret not having seen Père la Chaise once more, and the circus in the Champs-Élysées!”
“You are in a great hurry, then?”
“I am not, but my master is. By the way, I must buy some shoes and shirts. We came away without trunks, only with a carpet-bag.”
“I will show you an excellent shop for getting what you want.”
“Really, monsieur, you are very kind.”
And they walked off together, Passepartout chatting volubly as they went.
“Above all,” he said, “don’t let me lose the steamer.”
“You have plenty of time; it’s only twelve o’clock.”
Passepartout pulled out his big watch. “Twelve!” he exclaimed; “why, it’s only eight minutes before ten.”
“Your watch is slow.”
“My watch? A family watch, monsieur, that has come down from my great-grandfather! It doesn’t vary five minutes in the year. It’s a perfect chronometer, look you.”
“I see how it is,” said Fix. “You have kept London time, which is two hours behind that of Suez. You ought to regulate your watch at noon in each country.”
“I regulate my watch? Never!”
“Well, then, it won’t agree with the sun.”
“So much the worse for the sun, monsieur. The sun will be wrong, then!”
And the worthy fellow returned the watch to its fob with a defiant gesture. After a few minutes’ silence, Fix resumed: “You left London hastily, then?”
“I rather think so! Last Friday at eight o’clock in the evening, Monsieur Fogg came home from his club, and three-quarters of an hour afterwards we were off.”
“But where is your master going?”
“Always straight ahead. He is going round the world.”
“Round the world?” cried Fix.
“Yes, and in eighty days! He says it’s on a wager; but, between us, I don’t believe a word of it. That wouldn’t be common sense. There’s something else in the wind.”
“Ah! Mr. Fogg is a character, is he?”
“I should say he was.”
“Is he rich?”

“No doubt, for he is carrying an enormous sum in brand new banknotes with him. And he doesn’t spare the money on the way, either: he has offered a large reward to the engineer of the ‘Mongolia’ if he gets us to Bombay well ahead of time.”
“And you have known your master a long time?”
“Why, no; I entered his service the very day we left London.”

The effect of these replies on the already suspicious and excited detective can be imagined. The hasty departure from London soon after the robbery; the large sum carried by Mr. Fogg; his eagerness to reach distant countries; the pretext of an eccentric and foolhardy bet—all confirmed Fix in his theory. He continued to pump poor Passepartout, and learned that he really knew little or nothing of his master, who lived a solitary existence in London, was said to be rich though no one knew where his riches came from, and was mysterious and impenetrable in his affairs and habits. Fix felt sure that Phileas Fogg would not land at Suez, but was really going on to Bombay.
“Is Bombay far from here?” asked Passepartout.
“Pretty far. It’s a ten days’ voyage by sea.”
“And in what country is Bombay?”
“India.”
“In Asia?”
“Certainly.”
“The deuce! I was going to tell you—there’s one thing that worries me—my burner!”
“What burner?”

“My gas-burner, which I forgot to turn off, and which is burning at this moment at my expense. I have calculated, monsieur, that I lose two shillings every twenty-four hours, exactly sixpence more than I earn; and you will understand that the longer our journey—”

Did Fix pay any attention to Passepartout’s trouble about the gas? It is not likely. He was not listening, but turning a project over in his mind. Passepartout and he had now reached the shop, where Fix left his companion to make his purchases, after telling him not to miss the steamer, and hurried back to the consulate. Now that he was fully convinced, Fix had quite recovered his equanimity.
“Consul,” he said, “I have no longer any doubt. I have spotted my man. He passes himself off as an odd stick who is going round the world in eighty days.”
“Then he’s a sharp fellow,” returned the consul, “and counts on returning to London after putting the police of the two countries off his track.”
“We’ll see about that,” replied Fix.
“But are you not mistaken?”
“I am not mistaken.”
“Why was this robber so anxious to prove, by the _visa_, that he had passed through Suez?”
“Why? I have no idea; but listen to me.”
He reported in a few words the most important parts of his conversation with Passepartout.
“In short,” said the consul, “appearances are wholly against this man. And what are you going to do?”

“Send a dispatch to London for a warrant of arrest to be dispatched instantly to Bombay, take passage on board the ‘Mongolia,’ follow my rogue to India, and there, on English ground, arrest him politely, with my warrant in my hand and my hand on his shoulder.”

Having uttered these words with a cool, careless air, the detective took leave of the consul and went to the telegraph office, from which he sent the dispatch we have already seen to the London police office. A quarter of an hour later Fix, with a small bag in his hand, was making his way on board the “Mongolia”; and a few moments later the noble steamer rode out at full steam upon the waters of the Red Sea.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. In which the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean Prove Propitious to the Designs of Phileas Fogg
paragraphs: The distance between Suez and Aden is precisely thirteen hundred and ten miles, and the company’s regulations allow the steamers one hundred and thirty-eight hours in which to traverse it. The “Mongolia,” thanks to the vigorous exertions of the engineer, seemed likely—so rapid was her speed—to reach her destination considerably within that time. The greater part of the passengers from Brindisi were bound for India: some for Bombay, others for Calcutta by way of Bombay, which is now the nearest route thither, since a railway crosses the Indian peninsula. Among the passengers was a number of officials and military officers of various grades, the latter either attached to the regular British forces or commanding the Sepoy troops, and receiving high salaries ever since the central government took over the powers of the East India Company: sub-lieutenants get £280, brigadiers £2,400, and generals of divisions £4,000. What with the military men, a number of rich young Englishmen on their travels, and the hospitable efforts of the purser, the time passed quickly on the “Mongolia.” The best of fare was set out on the cabin tables at breakfast, lunch, dinner, and the eight o’clock supper; the ladies scrupulously changed their toilets twice a day; and the hours flew by, when the sea was tranquil, in music, dancing, and games.

But the Red Sea is full of caprice, and often boisterous, like most long, narrow gulfs. When the wind came from the African or Asian coast, the “Mongolia,” with her long hull, rolled fearfully. Then the ladies quickly disappeared below; the pianos were silent; singing and dancing suddenly ceased. Yet the good ship ploughed straight on, unhindered by wind or wave, towards the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb. What was Phileas Fogg doing all this time? It might be thought that, in his anxiety, he would be constantly watching the changes of the wind, the unruly raging of the billows—every chance, in short, which might force the “Mongolia” to slacken her speed and so interrupt his journey. But if he thought of these possibilities, he did not betray it by any outward sign.

Always the same impassive member of the Reform Club, whom no incident could surprise, as unvarying as the ship’s chronometers, seldom even curious enough to go on deck, he passed through the memorable scenes of the Red Sea with cold indifference; did not care to recognise the historic towns and villages whose picturesque outlines rose against the sky along its shores; and betrayed no fear of the dangers of the Arabian Gulf, of which the old historians always spoke with horror, and upon which the ancient navigators never ventured without propitiating the gods with ample sacrifices. How did this eccentric personage pass his time on the “Mongolia”? He took his four hearty meals every day, regardless of the most persistent rolling and pitching on the part of the steamer; and he played whist indefatigably, for he had found partners as enthusiastic about the game as himself. A tax-collector on the way to his post at Goa; the Rev. Decimus Smith, returning to his parish at Bombay; and a brigadier-general of the English army, who was about to rejoin his brigade at Benares, made up the party, and together with Mr. Fogg played whist by the hour in absorbing silence.

As for Passepartout, he too had escaped sea-sickness, and took his meals conscientiously in the forward cabin. He rather enjoyed the voyage, for he was well fed and well lodged, took a great interest in the scenes through which they were passing, and consoled himself with the delusion that his master’s whim would end at Bombay. He was pleased, the day after leaving Suez, to find on deck the obliging person with whom he had walked and chatted on the quays.
“If I am not mistaken,” he said, approaching this person with his most amiable smile, “you are the gentleman who so kindly volunteered to guide me at Suez?”
“Ah! I quite recognise you. You are the servant of the strange Englishman—”
“Just so, monsieur—”
“Fix.”
“Monsieur Fix,” resumed Passepartout, “I’m charmed to find you on board. Where are you bound?”
“Like you, to Bombay.”
“That’s capital! Have you made this trip before?”
“Several times. I am one of the agents of the Peninsular Company.”
“Then you know India?”
“Why yes,” replied Fix, who spoke cautiously.
“A curious place, this India?”
“Oh, very curious. Mosques, minarets, temples, fakirs, pagodas, tigers, snakes, elephants! I hope you will have ample time to see the sights.”

“I hope so, Monsieur Fix. You see, a man of sound sense ought not to spend his life jumping from a steamer onto a railway train, and from a railway train onto a steamer again, pretending to make the tour of the world in eighty days! No; all these gymnastics, you may be sure, will cease at Bombay.”
“And Mr. Fogg is getting on well?” asked Fix, in the most natural tone in the world.
“Quite well, and I too. I eat like a famished ogre; it’s the sea air.”
“But I never see your master on deck.”
“Never; he hasn’t the least curiosity.”
“Do you know, Mr. Passepartout, that this pretended tour in eighty days may conceal some secret errand—perhaps a diplomatic mission?”
“Faith, Monsieur Fix, I assure you I know nothing about it, nor would I give half a crown to find out.”

After this meeting, Passepartout and Fix got into the habit of chatting together, the latter making it a point to gain the worthy fellow’s confidence. He frequently offered him a glass of whiskey or pale ale in the steamer’s bar-room, which Passepartout never failed to accept with graceful alacrity, mentally pronouncing Fix the best of good fellows.

Meanwhile the “Mongolia” was pushing forward rapidly; on the 13th, Mocha, surrounded by its ruined walls on which date-trees were growing, came into sight, and on the mountains beyond vast coffee-fields could be made out. Passepartout was enchanted to behold this celebrated place, and thought that, with its circular walls and dismantled fort, it looked like an immense coffee-cup and saucer. The following night they passed through the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, which means in Arabic “The Bridge of Tears,” and the next day they put in at Steamer Point, north-west of Aden harbour, to take on coal. This matter of fuelling steamers is a serious one at such distances from the coal-mines; it costs the Peninsular Company some eight hundred thousand pounds a year. In these distant seas, coal is worth three or four pounds sterling a ton.

The “Mongolia” still had sixteen hundred and fifty miles to traverse before reaching Bombay, and had to remain four hours at Steamer Point to coal up. But this delay, as it had been foreseen, did not affect Phileas Fogg’s programme; besides, the “Mongolia,” instead of reaching Aden on the morning of the 15th as she was due, arrived there on the evening of the 14th, a gain of fifteen hours.

Mr. Fogg and his servant went ashore at Aden to have the passport _visaed_ again; Fix, unobserved, followed them. The _visa_ procured, Mr. Fogg returned on board to resume his former habits; while Passepartout, as usual, sauntered about among the mixed population of Somalis, Banyans, Parsees, Jews, Arabs, and Europeans who make up the twenty-five thousand inhabitants of Aden. He gazed with wonder at the fortifications which make this place the Gibraltar of the Indian Ocean, and at the vast cisterns where the English engineers were still at work, two thousand years after the engineers of Solomon.

“Very curious, _very_ curious,” said Passepartout to himself on returning to the steamer. “I see that it is by no means useless to travel, if a man wants to see something new.” At six p.m. the “Mongolia” slowly moved out of the roadstead, and was soon once more on the Indian Ocean. She had a hundred and sixty-eight hours in which to reach Bombay, and the sea was favourable, the wind being in the north-west, and all sails aiding the engine. The steamer rolled but little; the ladies, in fresh toilets, reappeared on deck; and the singing and dancing were resumed. The trip was being accomplished most successfully, and Passepartout was enchanted with the congenial companion chance had secured him in the person of the delightful Fix. On Sunday, October 20th, towards noon, they came in sight of the Indian coast: two hours later the pilot came on board. A range of hills lay against the sky on the horizon, and soon the rows of palms which adorn Bombay came distinctly into view. The steamer entered the road formed by the islands in the bay, and at half-past four she hauled up at the quays of Bombay.

Phileas Fogg was in the act of finishing the thirty-third rubber of the voyage, and his partner and himself, having by a bold stroke captured all thirteen of the tricks, concluded this fine campaign with a brilliant victory.

The “Mongolia” was due at Bombay on the 22nd; she arrived on the 20th. This was a gain to Phileas Fogg of two days since his departure from London, and he calmly entered the fact in the itinerary, in the column of gains.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. In which Passepartout is only too Glad to Get Off with the Loss of His Shoes
paragraphs: Everybody knows that the great reversed triangle of land, with its base in the north and its apex in the south, which is called India, takes in fourteen hundred thousand square miles, on which is spread, unevenly, a population of one hundred and eighty million souls. The British Crown exercises a real and despotic dominion over the larger portion of this vast country, and has a governor-general stationed at Calcutta, governors at Madras, Bombay, and in Bengal, and a lieutenant-governor at Agra.

But British India proper takes in only seven hundred thousand square miles, with a population of from one hundred to one hundred and ten million inhabitants. A considerable portion of India is still free from British authority; and there are certain ferocious rajahs in the interior who are absolutely independent. The celebrated East India Company was all-powerful from 1756, when the English first gained a foothold on the spot where the city of Madras now stands, down to the time of the great Sepoy insurrection. It gradually annexed province after province, purchasing them from the native chiefs, whom it seldom paid, and appointed the governor-general and his subordinates, civil and military. But the East India Company has now passed away, leaving the British possessions in India directly under the control of the Crown. The aspect of the country, as well as the manners and racial distinctions, is daily changing.

Formerly one was obliged to travel in India by the old cumbrous methods—going on foot or on horseback, in palanquins or unwieldy coaches; now fast steamboats ply on the Indus and the Ganges, and a great railway, with branch lines joining the main line at many points along its route, traverses the peninsula from Bombay to Calcutta in three days. This railway does not run in a direct line across India. The distance between Bombay and Calcutta, as the bird flies, is only from one thousand to eleven hundred miles; but the deflections of the road increase this distance by more than a third.

The general route of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway is as follows: leaving Bombay, it passes through Salcette, crossing to the continent opposite Tannah, goes over the chain of the Western Ghauts, runs thence north-east as far as Burhampoor, skirts the nearly independent territory of Bundelcund, ascends to Allahabad, turns thence eastward, meeting the Ganges at Benares, then departs from the river a little, and, descending south-eastward by Burdivan and the French town of Chandernagor, has its terminus at Calcutta.
The passengers of the “Mongolia” went ashore at half-past four p.m.; at exactly eight the train would start for Calcutta.

Mr. Fogg, after bidding good-bye to his whist partners, left the steamer, gave his servant several errands to do, urged him to be at the station promptly at eight, and, with his regular step which beat to the second like an astronomical clock, made his way to the passport office. As for the wonders of Bombay—its famous city hall, its splendid library, its forts and docks, its bazaars, mosques, synagogues, its Armenian churches, and the noble pagoda on Malabar Hill, with its two polygonal towers—he did not care a straw to see them. He would not deign to examine even the masterpieces of Elephanta, or the mysterious hypogea concealed south-east of the docks, or those fine remains of Buddhist architecture, the Kanherian grottoes of the island of Salcette.

Having transacted his business at the passport office, Phileas Fogg went quietly to the railway station, where he ordered dinner. Among the dishes served up to him, the landlord especially recommended a certain giblet of “native rabbit,” on which he prided himself.

Mr. Fogg accordingly tasted the dish, but, despite its spiced sauce, found it far from palatable. He rang for the landlord, and, when he appeared, said, fixing his clear eyes on him: “Is this rabbit, sir?”
“Yes, my lord,” the rogue boldly replied, “rabbit from the jungles.”
“And this rabbit did not mew when he was killed?”
“Mew, my lord! What, a rabbit mew! I swear to you—”
“Be so good, landlord, as not to swear, but remember this: cats were formerly considered, in India, as sacred animals. That was a good time.”
“For the cats, my lord?”
“Perhaps for the travellers as well!”

After which Mr. Fogg quietly continued his dinner. Fix had gone ashore shortly after Mr. Fogg, and his first destination was the headquarters of the Bombay police. He made himself known as a London detective, told his business at Bombay and the position of affairs concerning the supposed robber, and nervously asked whether a warrant had arrived from London. It had not reached the office; indeed, there had not yet been time for it to arrive. Fix was sorely disappointed, and tried to obtain an order of arrest from the director of the Bombay police. This the director refused, since the matter concerned the London office, which alone could legally deliver the warrant. Fix did not insist, and had to resign himself to wait for the arrival of the important document; but he was determined not to lose sight of the mysterious rogue as long as he stayed in Bombay. He did not doubt for a moment, any more than Passepartout did, that Phileas Fogg would remain there, at least until it was time for the warrant to arrive.

Passepartout, however, had no sooner heard his master’s orders on leaving the “Mongolia” than he saw at once that they were to leave Bombay as they had left Suez and Paris, and that the journey would be extended at least as far as Calcutta, and perhaps beyond. He began to ask himself whether this bet that Mr. Fogg talked about wasn’t really in good earnest, and whether his fate wasn’t truly forcing him, despite his love of repose, round the world in eighty days!

Having bought the usual quota of shirts and shoes, he took a leisurely stroll about the streets, where crowds of people of many nationalities—Europeans, Persians with pointed caps, Banyas with round turbans, Sindes with square bonnets, Parsees with black mitres, and long-robed Armenians—were gathered. It happened to be the day of a Parsee festival. These descendants of the sect of Zoroaster—the most thrifty, civilised, intelligent, and austere of the East Indians, among whom are counted the richest native merchants of Bombay—were celebrating a sort of religious carnival, with processions and shows, in the midst of which Indian dancing-girls, clothed in rose-coloured gauze, looped up with gold and silver, danced airily, but with perfect modesty, to the sound of viols and the clanging of tambourines. Needless to say, Passepartout watched these curious ceremonies with staring eyes and gaping mouth, and his countenance was that of the greenest booby imaginable.

Unhappily for his master, as well as for himself, his curiosity drew him unconsciously farther off than he had meant to go. At last, having seen the Parsee carnival wind away into the distance, he was turning his steps towards the station when he happened to catch sight of the splendid pagoda on Malabar Hill, and was seized with an irresistible desire to see its interior. He was quite ignorant that it is forbidden to Christians to enter certain Indian temples, and that even the faithful must not go in without first leaving their shoes outside the door. It may be said here that the wise policy of the British Government severely punishes any disregard of the practices of the native religions.

Passepartout, however, thinking no harm, went in like a simple tourist, and was soon lost in admiration of the splendid Brahmin ornamentation that met his eyes on every side, when of a sudden he found himself sprawling on the sacred flagging. He looked up to see three enraged priests, who at once fell upon him, tore off his shoes, and began to beat him with loud, savage exclamations. The agile Frenchman was soon on his feet again, and lost no time in knocking down two of his long-gowned adversaries with his fists and a vigorous application of his toes; then, rushing out of the pagoda as fast as his legs could carry him, he soon escaped the third priest by mingling with the crowd in the streets.
At five minutes before eight, Passepartout, hatless, shoeless, and having in the squabble lost his package of shirts and shoes, rushed breathlessly into the station.

Fix, who had followed Mr. Fogg to the station and saw that he was really going to leave Bombay, was there, on the platform. He had resolved to follow the supposed robber to Calcutta, and farther, if necessary. Passepartout did not notice the detective, who stood in an obscure corner; but Fix heard him relate his adventures in a few words to Mr. Fogg.

“I hope this will not happen again,” said Phileas Fogg coldly, as he got into the train. Poor Passepartout, quite crestfallen, followed his master without a word. Fix was on the point of entering another carriage when an idea struck him which made him change his plan.
“No, I’ll stay,” he muttered. “An offence has been committed on Indian soil. I’ve got my man.”
Just then the locomotive gave a sharp screech, and the train passed out into the darkness of the night.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. In which Phileas Fogg Secures a Curious Means of Conveyance at a Fabulous Price
paragraphs: Toget var afgået til tiden. Blandt passagererne var en række officerer, embedsmænd samt opium- og indigokøbmænd, hvis forretninger kaldte dem til østkysten. Passepartout sad i samme kupé som sin herre, og en tredje passager sad på sædet over for dem. Det var Sir Francis Cromarty, en af Mr. Foggs whistpartnere fra »Mongolia«, nu på vej tilbage til sit korps i Benares. Sir Francis var en høj, lys mand på halvtreds, som havde udmærket sig stort under det sidste Sepoy-oprør. Han havde gjort Indien til sit hjem og aflagde kun korte og sjældne besøg i England, og var næsten lige så fortrolig som en indfødt med Indiens skikke, historie og folkets karakter. Men Phileas Fogg, der ikke rejste, men blot trak en cirkellinje, gjorde sig ingen ulejlighed med at undersøge slige ting. Han var et fast legeme, der bevægede sig ad sin bane omkring jordkloden ifølge den rationelle mekaniks love. I selvsamme øjeblik regnede han i hovedet på, hvor mange timer der var gået siden afrejsen fra London, og havde det ligget til hans natur at gøre sig til, ville han have gnedet sig i hænderne af tilfredshed. Sir Francis Cromarty havde lagt mærke til sin rejsefælles besynderlighed — skønt han kun havde haft lejlighed til at studere ham mellem kortgivningerne og mellem to robberter — og han spurgte sig selv, om et menneskehjerte virkelig slog under denne kolde overflade, og om Phileas Fogg overhovedet havde sans for naturens skønhed. Brigadegeneralen kunne mellem sig selv godt indrømme, at af alle de excentriske personer han nogensinde havde mødt, kunne ingen måle sig med dette produkt af de eksakte videnskaber.

Phileas Fogg havde ikke skjult for Sir Francis sin plan om at rejse jorden rundt eller de omstændigheder, hvorunder han var draget af sted. Generalen så i væddemålet kun en unyttig excentricitet og en mangel på sund fornuft. Som denne mærkelige gentleman bar sig ad, ville han forlade verden uden at have gjort hverken sig selv eller andre noget godt.

En time efter afrejsen fra Bombay havde toget passeret viadukterne og øen Salcette og var nået ud på det åbne land. Ved Callyan kom de til skæringspunktet med sidebanen, der løber ned mod det sydøstlige Indien gennem Kandallah og Pounah. Forbi Pauwell kørte de ind i bjergpassene med deres basaltsokler og toppe kronet af tætte, grønne skove. Phileas Fogg og Sir Francis Cromarty vekslede et par ord i ny og næ, og nu tog Sir Francis tråden op igen og bemærkede: »For nogle år siden, Mr. Fogg, ville De være løbet ind i en forsinkelse netop her, der formodentlig havde kostet Dem væddemålet.«
»Hvordan det, Sir Francis?«
»Fordi jernbanen standsede ved foden af disse bjerge, og passagererne måtte krydse dem i palankiner eller på ponyer for at nå Kandallah på den anden side.«
»En sådan forsinkelse ville ikke have forrykket mine planer det mindste,« sagde Mr. Fogg. »Jeg har altid forudset muligheden af visse hindringer.«

»Men, Mr. Fogg,« fortsatte Sir Francis, »De risikerer at få vrøvl på grund af denne brave karls eventyr ved pagoden.« Passepartout havde lunt svøbt fødderne i sit rejsetæppe og sov tungt og anede ikke, at man talte om ham. »Regeringen er meget streng over for den slags forseelser. Den er særlig opmærksom på, at indernes religiøse skikke respekteres, og hvis Deres tjener var blevet pågrebet —«

»Ganske vist, Sir Francis,« svarede Mr. Fogg. »Hvis han var blevet pågrebet, ville han være blevet dømt og straffet, og bagefter var han stille og roligt rejst tilbage til Europa. Jeg kan ikke se, hvordan denne sag skulle kunne have forsinket hans herre.«

Samtalen gik i stå igen. I løbet af natten lagde toget bjergene bag sig og passerede Nassik, og næste dag rullede det videre over Khandeishs flade, veldyrkede land med dets spredte landsbyer, over hvilke pagodernes minareter rejste sig. Denne frugtbare egn vandes af talrige små floder og klare vandløb, hvoraf de fleste er bifloder til Godavery.

Passepartout kunne, da han vågnede og kiggede ud, ikke fatte, at han virkelig krydsede Indien i et jernbanetog. Lokomotivet, der blev kørt af en engelsk maskinmester og fyret med engelsk kul, sendte sin røg ud over plantager af bomuld, kaffe, muskat, nelliker og peber, mens dampen krusede sig i spiraler omkring klynger af palmer, hvori der dukkede maleriske bungalower op, viharier (en slags forladte klostre) og vidunderlige templer beriget med den indiske arkitekturs uudtømmelige ornamentik. Derefter kom de ud over vidtstrakte sletter, der nåede til horisonten, med jungler beboet af slanger og tigre, som flygtede ved togets støj, fulgt af skove, gennemskåret af jernbanen og stadig hjemsøgt af elefanter, der betragtede det forbifarende tog med tankefulde øjne. Hinsides Milligaum krydsede de rejsende det dødbringende land, så ofte plettet med blod af gudinden Kalis tilbedere. Ikke langt borte rejste Ellora sig med sine yndefulde pagoder og det berømte Aurungabad, hovedstad i den grusomme Aureng-Zebs rige, nu hovedstad i en af de udskilte provinser i Nizamens kongerige. Det var her i egnen, at Feringhea, thugernes høvding, kvælernes konge, engang havde hersket. Disse skurke, bundet af en hemmelig ed, kvalte ofre i enhver alder til ære for dødens gudinde, uden nogensinde at udgyde en bloddråbe. Der var en tid, da man dårligt kunne krydse denne del af landet uden at lig dukkede op til alle sider. Den engelske regering har formået at nedbringe disse mord betydeligt, men thugerne findes stadig og praktiserer fortsat deres rædselsfulde riter.

Klokken halv et standsede toget i Burhampoor, hvor Passepartout kunne købe sig et par indiske tøfler, prydet med uægte perler, hvori han med tydelig forfængelighed straks indhyllede sine fødder. De rejsende indtog en hastig frokost og drog videre mod Assurghur, efter at de et stykke vej havde fulgt bredden af den lille flod Tapty, som munder ud i Cambraybugten nær Surat.

Passepartout var nu sunket ned i en altopslugende grublen. Indtil ankomsten til Bombay havde han håbet, at rejsen ville ende der; men nu da de tydeligvis fór for fuld fart tværs over Indien, havde stemningen i hans dagdrømme pludselig skiftet. Hans gamle vagabondnatur kom tilbage til ham; hans ungdoms fantastiske ideer fik atter tag i ham.
