Han begyndte at betragte sin herres plan som blodig alvor, at tro på væddemålets realitet og dermed på rejsen jorden rundt og nødvendigheden af at fuldføre den inden for den fastsatte tid. Han var allerede begyndt at bekymre sig om mulige forsinkelser og uheld undervejs. Han følte sig personligt indviklet i væddemålet og rystede ved tanken om, at han kunne have været årsag til, at det blev tabt, gennem sin utilgivelige dårskab aftenen forinden. Langt mindre koldblodig end Mr. Fogg var han langt mere urolig, talte og talte igen de dage, der var gået, bandede hver gang toget standsede, beskyldte det for sløvhed og bebrejdede i stilhed Mr. Fogg, at han ikke havde bestukket maskinmesteren. Den brave fyr havde ingen anelse om, at sådanne metoder vel kunne sætte fart i en damper, men ikke virkede på en jernbane.

Henimod aften kørte toget ind i passene gennem Sutpour-bjergene, der adskiller Khandeish fra Bundelcund. Næste dag spurgte Sir Francis Cromarty Passepartout, hvad klokken var, hvorpå denne efter at have set på sit ur svarede, at den var tre om morgenen. Dette berømte stykke urværk, der altid var stillet efter Greenwich-meridianen — som nu lå omkring syvoghalvfjerds grader vestpå — gik mindst fire timer for sent. Sir Francis korrigerede Passepartouts tid, hvorpå Passepartout fremsatte samme bemærkning, som han havde fremsat over for Fix. Da generalen insisterede på, at uret burde stilles ved hver ny meridian, eftersom han hele tiden rejste østpå, det vil sige solen i møde, og dagene følgelig var fire minutter kortere for hver grad de krydsede, nægtede Passepartout halsstarrigt at ændre sit ur, som han holdt på London-tid. Det var en uskyldig vrangforestilling, der ikke kunne skade nogen.

Klokken otte standsede toget midt i en lysning omkring femten miles forbi Rothal, hvor der lå flere bungalower og arbejderboliger. Konduktøren gik langs vognene og råbte: »Passagererne stiger af her!«
Phileas Fogg så på Sir Francis Cromarty efter en forklaring, men generalen kunne ikke sige, hvad der havde standset dem midt i denne skov af daddelpalmer og akacier.
Passepartout, der ikke var mindre forundret, styrtede ud og kom hurtigt tilbage med et udbrud: »Monsieur, ikke mere jernbane!«
»Hvad mener De?« spurgte Sir Francis.
»Jeg mener, at toget ikke kører videre.«
Generalen trådte straks ud, mens Phileas Fogg roligt fulgte ham, og sammen gik de hen til konduktøren.
»Hvor er vi?« spurgte Sir Francis.
»Ved landsbyen Kholby.«
»Standser vi her?«
»Bestemt. Jernbanen er ikke færdig.«
»Hvad! Ikke færdig?«
»Nej. Der mangler endnu omkring halvtreds miles at lægge herfra til Allahabad, hvor linjen begynder igen.«
»Men aviserne meddelte, at jernbanen var åbnet i hele sin længde.«
»Hvad vil De have, hr. officer? Aviserne tog fejl.«
»Men De sælger billetter fra Bombay til Calcutta,« replicerede Sir Francis ophidset.
»Givet,« svarede konduktøren; »men passagererne ved, at de selv må sørge for transport fra Kholby til Allahabad.«
Sir Francis var rasende. Passepartout ville gladelig have slået konduktøren omkuld og turde ikke se sin herre i øjnene.
»Sir Francis,« sagde Mr. Fogg roligt, »vi vil, om De vil, se os om efter en eller anden transportmulighed til Allahabad.«
»Mr. Fogg, dette er en forsinkelse, der i høj grad falder Dem til ulempe.«
»Nej, Sir Francis; den var forudset.«
»Hvad! Vidste De da, at banen —«

»Slet ikke; men jeg vidste, at en eller anden hindring før eller siden ville dukke op på min rute. Intet er derfor tabt. Jeg har to dage, som jeg allerede har vundet, at ofre. En damper afgår fra Calcutta til Hong Kong middag den 25. I dag er det den 22., og vi vil nå Calcutta i tide.«
Der var intet at svare på et så sikkert svar.

Det var kun alt for sandt, at jernbanen endte her. Aviserne lignede visse ure, der har en vane med at gå for hurtigt, og de havde været forhastede med at melde linjen for færdig. De fleste rejsende kendte til dette brud, og da de stod af toget, gav de sig til at leje, hvad landsbyen kunne stille af køretøjer: firehjulede palki-gharier, vogne trukket af zebuer, vogne der lignede pagoder på vandring, palankiner, ponyer og hvad ved jeg.
Mr. Fogg og Sir Francis Cromarty kom tilbage efter at have gennemsøgt landsbyen fra ende til anden uden at have fundet noget.
»Jeg går til fods,« sagde Phileas Fogg.

Passepartout, som lige var stødt til sin herre, skar en sur grimasse, da han kom til at tænke på sine pragtfulde, men alt for skrøbelige indiske sko. Heldigvis havde han også selv set sig om, og efter et øjebliks tøven sagde han: »Monsieur, jeg tror, jeg har fundet et middel til befordring.«
»Hvilket?«
»En elefant! En elefant tilhørende en inder, der bor ikke hundrede skridt herfra.«
»Lad os gå hen og se på elefanten,« svarede Mr. Fogg.

De nåede snart en lille hytte, og nær ved den, indhegnet af høje stakitter, stod det omtalte dyr. En inder kom ud af hytten og førte dem på deres anmodning ind i indhegningen. Elefanten, som dens ejer ikke havde opdrættet som lastdyr, men til krigsbrug, var halvt tæmmet. Inderen havde allerede begyndt, ved hyppigt at irritere ham og fodre ham hver tredje måned med sukker og smør, at give ham en vildskab, der var hans natur fremmed — en metode, der ofte anvendes af dem, der træner indiske elefanter til kamp. Heldigvis for Mr. Fogg var dyrets afretning i den retning dog ikke nået langt, og elefanten bevarede endnu sin naturlige mildhed. Kiouni — således hed dyret — kunne uden tvivl tilbagelægge store strækninger hurtigt, og i mangel af andre befordringsmidler besluttede Mr. Fogg at leje ham. Men elefanter er langtfra billige i Indien, hvor de bliver sjældne. Hannerne, som alene egner sig til cirkusforestillinger, er meget eftertragtede, så meget mere som kun få af dem er tæmmede. Da Mr. Fogg derfor foreslog at leje Kiouni, gav inderen et blankt afslag. Mr. Fogg holdt fast, idet han tilbød den ekstravagante sum af ti pund i timen for at låne dyret til Allahabad. Afslag. Tyve pund? Afslag også. Fyrre pund? Stadig afslag. Passepartout hoppede ved hvert nyt tilbud; men inderen lod sig ikke friste. Og dog var tilbuddet fristende, for hvis elefanten brugte femten timer på at nå Allahabad, ville dens ejer modtage ikke mindre end seks hundrede pund sterling.

Phileas Fogg, uden at lade sig forrykke det mindste, foreslog da at købe dyret regelret og tilbød først tusind pund for ham. Inderen, som måske troede at være på vej til at gøre en god handel, gav stadig afslag.

Sir Francis Cromarty tog Mr. Fogg til side og bad ham betænke sig, før han gik videre. Gentlemanen svarede, at det ikke lå til ham at handle overilet, at et væddemål på tyve tusind pund stod på spil, at elefanten var ham absolut nødvendig, og at han ville sikre sig ham, om så han skulle betale tyve gange dens værdi. Han vendte tilbage til inderen, hvis små, skarpe øjne, glinsende af grådighed, viste, at det for ham kun var et spørgsmål om, hvor høj en pris han kunne få, og Mr. Fogg bød først tolv hundrede, så femten hundrede, atten hundrede, to tusind pund. Passepartout, ellers så rødmosset, var nu hvid i ansigtet af spænding.
Ved to tusind pund gav inderen efter.
»Hvilken pris, gode himmel!« udbrød Passepartout, »for en elefant.«

Det stod nu kun tilbage at finde en fører, hvilket var forholdsvis let. En ung Parsi med et intelligent ansigt tilbød sine tjenester, hvilket Mr. Fogg tog imod og lovede ham en så rundhåndet belønning, at det betydeligt skærpede hans iver. Elefanten blev ført ud og rustet til rejsen. Parsien, en dreven elefantfører, dækkede dens ryg med en slags sadeltæppe og fastgjorde til hver af dens flanker en af de besynderlig ubekvemme howdaher. Phileas Fogg betalte inderen med nogle pengesedler, som han trak frem af den berømte rejsetaske, en handling der syntes at vride hjertet ud af stakkels Passepartout. Derefter tilbød han at føre Sir Francis til Allahabad, en indbydelse brigadegeneralen taknemmeligt tog imod, da én rejsende mere næppe ville udmatte det gigantiske dyr. Forsyninger blev indkøbt i Kholby, og mens Sir Francis og Mr. Fogg tog plads i hver sin howdah, satte Passepartout sig overskrævs på sadeltæppet mellem dem. Parsien tog plads på elefantens nakke, og klokken ni drog de ud af landsbyen, idet dyret skred af sted gennem den tætte palmeskov ad den korteste vej.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. In which Phileas Fogg and His Companions Venture Across the Indian Forests, and What Ensued
paragraphs: For at forkorte rejsen holdt føreren sig til venstre for den linje, hvor jernbanen endnu var under bygning. Denne linje fulgte ikke en lige kurs på grund af Vindhia-bjergenes lunefulde svingninger. Parsien, som var grundigt fortrolig med egnens veje og stier, erklærede, at de ville vinde tyve miles ved at skyde lige tværs gennem skoven.

Phileas Fogg og Sir Francis Cromarty, sænket op til halsen i de besynderlige howdaher, der var stillet til rådighed for dem, blev gyseligt rystet af elefantens hurtige trav, drevet frem af den dygtige Parsi; men de bar ubehaget med ægte britisk flegma, talte lidt og kunne knap få et glimt af hinanden. Hvad Passepartout angik, som sad oven på dyret og fik den fulde kraft af hvert stød, mens elefanten skred af sted, passede han nøje på, som hans herre havde rådet ham til, at holde tungen væk fra tænderne, da den ellers ville være blevet bidt rent af. Den brave fyr hoppede fra elefantens nakke til dens lænd og slog volter som en klovn på en springbræt; alligevel lo han midt under sine spring og tog fra tid til anden et stykke sukker op af lommen og stak det ned i Kiounis snabel, som tog imod det uden at slække sit jævne trav det mindste.

Efter to timer standsede føreren elefanten og gav ham en times hvil, hvorunder Kiouni, efter at have slukket sin tørst ved en nærliggende kilde, kastede sig over at fortære grene og buske omkring sig. Hverken Sir Francis eller Mr. Fogg fortrød pausen, og begge steg ned med en følelse af lettelse. »Han er sandelig af jern!« udbrød generalen og betragtede Kiouni beundrende.
»Af smedet jern,« svarede Passepartout, mens han gav sig i lag med at lave en hastig frokost.

Klokken tolv gav Parsien signal til afgang. Egnen antog snart et meget vildt præg. Krat af daddelpalmer og dværgpalmer veg for tætte skove, derpå for vidtstrakte, tørre sletter besat med spredte buske og overstrøet med store blokke af syenit. Hele denne del af Bundelcund, som sjældent besøges af rejsende, er beboet af en fanatisk befolkning hærdet i hindu-troens mest rædselsfulde praksisser. Englænderne har ikke kunnet skaffe sig fuld herredømme over dette område, der står under indflydelse af rajaher, som det er næsten umuligt at nå frem til i deres utilgængelige bjergborge. Flere gange fik de rejsende øje på flokke af voldsomme indere, der ved synet af elefanten, der skred tværs over landet, gjorde vrede og truende fagter. Parsien undgik dem så vidt muligt. Få dyr var at se langs ruten; selv aberne skyndte sig væk fra deres vej med fortrukne miner og grimasser, der fik Passepartout til at folde sig sammen af latter.

Midt i sin munterhed plagede dog en tanke den brave tjener. Hvad ville Mr. Fogg gøre med elefanten, når han nåede Allahabad? Ville han tage ham med videre? Umuligt! Omkostningerne ved at transportere ham ville gøre ham ruinerende dyr. Ville han sælge ham eller sætte ham fri? Det agtværdige dyr fortjente sandelig en vis omtanke. Hvis Mr. Fogg valgte at forære ham, Passepartout, Kiouni, ville han stå svært bekvemt; og disse tanker plagede ham længe.

Hovedkæden af Vindhia-bjergene var krydset ved otte om aftenen, og endnu et hvil blev gjort på nordskråningen i en forfalden bungalow. De havde tilbagelagt knap femogtyve miles den dag, og en lige så lang strækning lå endnu mellem dem og stationen i Allahabad.

Natten var kold. Parsien tændte et bål i bungalowen med et par tørre grene, og varmen var højst velkommen. Forsyninger købt i Kholby slog til som aftensmad, og de rejsende spiste glubsk. Samtalen, der begyndte med et par usammenhængende sætninger, gav snart plads til høje og jævne snorken. Føreren holdt vagt over Kiouni, som sov stående og støttede sig mod stammen af et stort træ. Intet hændte i løbet af natten, der kunne forstyrre de sovende, skønt lejlighedsvise brøl fra pantere og abers skvalder brød stilheden; de mere frygtindgydende dyr afgav hverken skrig eller fjendtlige tegn mod bungalowens beboere. Sir Francis sov tungt som en hæderlig soldat overvældet af træthed. Passepartout var indhyllet i urolige drømme om dagens hopperi. Hvad Mr. Fogg angik, slumrede han lige så fredeligt, som havde han ligget i sin rolige villa i Saville Row.

Rejsen blev genoptaget klokken seks om morgenen; føreren håbede at nå Allahabad til aften. I så fald ville Mr. Fogg kun miste en del af de otteogfyrre timer, han havde vundet siden rejsens begyndelse. Kiouni satte atter sin hurtige gang i gang og kom snart ned ad Vindhia-bjergenes lavere udløbere, og henimod middag passerede de landsbyen Kallenger ved Cani, en af Ganges' bifloder. Føreren undgik beboede steder, idet han fandt det sikrere at holde sig til det åbne land, der ligger langs de første sænkninger i den store flods bassin. Allahabad lå nu kun tolv miles nordøstpå. De gjorde ophold under en klynge af bananplanter, hvis frugt, lige så sund som brød og lige så saftig som fløde, blev spist i rigelige mængder og højt værdsat.

Klokken to red føreren ind i en tæt skov, der strakte sig flere miles; han foretrak at færdes under skovens skjul. Hidtil havde de ikke haft nogen ubehagelige møder, og rejsen syntes lige ved at blive fuldført med held, da elefanten, der blev urolig, pludselig standsede.
Klokken var da fire.
»Hvad er der i vejen?« spurgte Sir Francis og stak hovedet ud.
»Jeg ved ikke, hr. officer,« svarede Parsien og lyttede opmærksomt til en forvirret mumlen, der trængte igennem de tætte grene.

Mumlen blev snart tydeligere; den lød nu som et fjernt kor af menneskestemmer, ledsaget af blæseinstrumenter. Passepartout var lutter øjne og ører. Mr. Fogg ventede tålmodigt uden et ord. Parsien sprang til jorden, bandt elefanten til et træ og kastede sig ind i krattet. Han kom snart tilbage og sagde:
»En procession af brahminer kommer denne vej. Vi må forhindre, at de ser os, om muligt.«

Føreren løste elefanten og førte den ind i et krat, samtidig med at han bad de rejsende om ikke at røre sig. Han holdt sig parat til at bestige dyret med et øjebliks varsel, skulle flugt blive nødvendig; men han mente tydeligvis, at de troendes procession ville passere uden at lægge mærke til dem mellem det tætte løv, hvor de var fuldstændig skjult.

De disharmoniske lyde af stemmer og instrumenter nærmede sig, og nu blandede dybe sange sig med larmen fra tamburiner og bækkener. Processionens spids viste sig snart under træerne hundrede skridt borte, og de mærkelige skikkelser, der udførte den religiøse ceremoni, kunne let skelnes gennem grenene. Forrest gik præsterne med mitra på hovedet og iført lange dragter af kniplinger. De var omgivet af mænd, kvinder og børn, der istemte en slags klagende salme, brudt med regelmæssige mellemrum af tamburinerne og bækkenerne; mens der bag dem blev trukket en vogn med store hjul, hvis eger forestillede slanger snoet om hinanden. På vognen, der blev trukket af fire rigt udstafferede zebuer, stod en afskyelig statue med fire arme, dens krop farvet i en mat rød, med vildtstirrende øjne, uredt hår, fremstrakt tunge og læber farvet med betel. Den stod oprejst på skikkelsen af en udstrakt og hovedløs kæmpe.
Sir Francis genkendte statuen og hviskede: »Gudinden Kali; kærlighedens og dødens gudinde.«
»Dødens, måske,« mumlede Passepartout til svar, »men kærlighedens — den grimme gamle heks? Aldrig!«
Parsien gav tegn til tavshed.

En flok gamle fakirer hoppede omkring og lavede vild ståhej rundt om statuen; de var stribet med okker og dækket af snit, hvorfra blodet sivede dråbe for dråbe — dumme fanatikere, som ved de store indiske ceremonier endnu kaster sig under Juggernauts hjul. Nogle brahminer, klædt i Orientens fulde pragt, fulgte efter og førte en kvinde, der vaklede ved hvert skridt. Denne kvinde var ung og lige så lys som en europæer. Hendes hoved og hals, skuldre, øren, arme, hænder og tæer var tynget af smykker og ædelstene — af armbånd, øreringe og ringe; mens en tunika kantet med guld og dækket af en let muslindragt antydede konturen af hendes skikkelse.

Vagterne, der fulgte efter den unge kvinde, dannede en voldsom kontrast til hende, bevæbnet som de var med blanke sabler hængende ved hofterne og lange damaskerede pistoler, og bærende et lig på en palankin. Det var liget af en gammel mand, prægtigt klædt i en rajahs dragt og iført, som i live, en turban broderet med perler, en kappe af silke- og guldvævning, et skærf af kashmir besat med diamanter og en hindufyrstes pragtfulde våben. Derpå fulgte musikerne og en bagtrop af springende fakirer, hvis råb til tider overdøvede larmen fra instrumenterne; disse afsluttede processionen.
Sir Francis fulgte processionen med sorgfuldt åsyn og vendte sig mod føreren og sagde: »En suttee.«

Parsien nikkede og lagde fingeren på læben. Processionen snoede sig langsomt videre under træerne, og snart forsvandt dens sidste rækker i skovens dyb. Sangene døde gradvist hen; lejlighedsvise råb hørtes i det fjerne, indtil endelig alt igen var stilhed.
Phileas Fogg havde hørt, hvad Sir Francis sagde, og spurgte, så snart processionen var forsvundet: »Hvad er en suttee?«
»En suttee,« svarede generalen, »er et menneskeoffer, men et frivilligt et. Kvinden, De netop har set, vil i morgen ved daggry blive brændt.«
»Oh, de skurke!« udbrød Passepartout, som ikke kunne tilbageholde sin harme.
»Og liget?« spurgte Mr. Fogg.
»Det er fyrstens, hendes ægtemand,« sagde føreren; »en uafhængig rajah af Bundelcund.«

»Er det muligt,« fortsatte Phileas Fogg, og hans stemme røbede ikke den ringeste bevægelse, »at sådanne barbariske skikke stadig findes i Indien, og at englænderne ikke har formået at sætte en stopper for dem?«

»Disse ofringer forekommer ikke over den største del af Indien,« svarede Sir Francis; »men vi har ingen magt over disse vilde områder, og særlig ikke her i Bundelcund. Hele distriktet nord for Vindhia-bjergene er skueplads for uophørligt mord og plyndring.«
»Det stakkels væsen!« udbrød Passepartout, »at blive brændt levende!«

»Ja,« svarede Sir Francis, »brændt levende. Og blev hun ikke det, kan De ikke forestille Dem den slags behandling, hun ville være nødt til at underkaste sig fra sine slægtninges side. De ville rage hendes hår af, brødføde hende på et knapt mål ris, behandle hende med foragt; hun ville blive betragtet som et urent væsen og dø i en krog som en skabet hund. Udsigten til en så grufuld tilværelse driver disse stakkels skabninger til ofringen langt mere end kærlighed eller religiøs fanatisme. Undertiden er ofringen dog virkelig frivillig, og det kræver aktiv indgriben fra regeringen at forhindre den. For flere år siden, da jeg boede i Bombay, bad en ung enke guvernøren om tilladelse til at blive brændt sammen med sin mands lig; men som De kan tænke Dem, afslog han. Kvinden forlod byen, søgte tilflugt hos en uafhængig rajah og udførte dér sit selvopofrende forsæt.«
Mens Sir Francis talte, rystede føreren flere gange på hovedet og sagde nu: »Den ofring, der finder sted i morgen ved daggry, er ikke frivillig.«
»Hvordan ved De det?«
»Enhver i Bundelcund kender denne sag.«
»Men det ulykkelige væsen syntes ikke at gøre nogen modstand,« bemærkede Sir Francis.
»Det var, fordi de havde bedøvet hende med dampe af hamp og opium.«
»Men hvor fører de hende hen?«
»Til pagoden i Pillaji, to miles herfra; hun skal tilbringe natten der.«
»Og ofringen vil finde sted —«
»I morgen ved daggryets første lys.«

Føreren førte nu elefanten ud af krattet og sprang op på dens nakke. Netop som han skulle til at drive Kiouni frem med en særegen fløjten, standsede Mr. Fogg ham, vendte sig mod Sir Francis Cromarty og sagde: »Hvad om vi reddede denne kvinde.«
»Redde kvinden, Mr. Fogg!«
»Jeg har stadig tolv timer at undvære; jeg kan ofre dem til det.«
»Sandelig, De er en mand med hjerte!«
»Til tider,« svarede Phileas Fogg roligt; »når jeg har tid.«

chapters.title: Chapter 13. In which Passepartout Receives a New Proof that Fortune Favors the Brave
paragraphs: The plan was a bold one, full of difficulty, perhaps impossible. Mr. Fogg was about to risk his life, or at least his liberty, and with it the success of his tour. But he did not hesitate, and he found in Sir Francis Cromarty an enthusiastic ally.
As for Passepartout, he was ready for anything that might be proposed. His master's idea charmed him; he sensed a heart, a soul, beneath that icy exterior. He was beginning to love Phileas Fogg.
There remained the guide: what course would he take? Would he not side with the Indians? Failing his help, they needed at least to be sure of his neutrality.
Sir Francis put the question to him frankly.
"Officers," replied the guide, "I am a Parsee, and this woman is a Parsee. Command me as you will."
"Excellent!" said Mr. Fogg.
"However," the guide went on, "it is certain that we shall risk not only our lives, but horrible tortures, if we are caught."
"That is foreseen," replied Mr. Fogg. "I think we must wait till night before acting."
"I think so," said the guide.

The worthy Indian then gave some account of the victim. She was, he said, a celebrated beauty of the Parsee race and the daughter of a wealthy Bombay merchant. She had received a thoroughly English education in that city, and from her manners and intelligence would be taken for a European. Her name was Aouda. Left an orphan, she had been married against her will to the old rajah of Bundelcund; and, knowing the fate that awaited her, she had escaped, been recaptured, and condemned by the rajah's relatives—who had an interest in her death—to the sacrifice from which it seemed she could not escape.

The Parsee's narrative only strengthened Mr. Fogg and his companions in their generous plan. It was decided that the guide should steer the elephant toward the pagoda of Pillaji, which he accordingly approached as quickly as possible. Half an hour later they halted in a copse some five hundred feet from the pagoda, where they were well concealed; but they could hear the groans and cries of the fakirs distinctly.

They then discussed how to get at the victim. The guide was familiar with the pagoda of Pillaji, in which, he declared, the young woman was imprisoned. Could they enter one of its doors while the whole party of Indians lay in a drunken sleep, or was it safer to try to make a hole in the walls? That could only be decided on the spot and at the moment; but it was certain that the abduction must be made that very night, not when the victim was led to her funeral pyre at break of day. Then no human intervention could save her.

As soon as night fell, around six o'clock, they decided to make a reconnaissance around the pagoda. The cries of the fakirs were just ceasing; the Indians were in the act of sinking into the drunkenness produced by liquid opium mingled with hemp, and it might be possible to slip between them to the temple itself.

The Parsee, leading the others, crept noiselessly through the wood, and in ten minutes they found themselves on the banks of a small stream, from which, by the light of the rosin torches, they could make out a pyre of wood, on top of which lay the embalmed body of the rajah, which was to be burned with his wife. The pagoda, whose minarets loomed above the trees in the deepening dusk, stood a hundred steps away.
"Come!" whispered the guide.
He slipped through the brush more cautiously than ever, followed by his companions; the silence around them was broken only by the low murmuring of the wind among the branches.

Soon the Parsee stopped on the edge of the glade, which was lit up by the torches. The ground was covered by groups of Indians, motionless in their drunken sleep; it looked like a battlefield strewn with the dead. Men, women, and children lay together.

In the background, among the trees, the pagoda of Pillaji loomed distinctly. Much to the guide's disappointment, the rajah's guards, lit by torches, were watching at the doors and marching to and fro with bare sabres; and the priests, no doubt, were watching within as well.

The Parsee, now satisfied that it was impossible to force an entrance to the temple, advanced no farther but led his companions back. Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty also saw that nothing could be attempted on that side. They stopped, and held a whispered consultation.
"It is only eight now," said the brigadier, "and these guards may go to sleep too."
"It is not impossible," replied the Parsee.
They lay down at the foot of a tree and waited.

The time seemed long; the guide kept leaving them to look out from the edge of the wood, but the guards watched steadily by the glare of the torches, and a dim light crept through the windows of the pagoda.

They waited till midnight; but no change came over the guards, and it became clear that they could not be counted on to give in to sleep. The other plan must be carried out: an opening in the walls of the pagoda must be made. The question remained whether the priests were keeping watch beside their victim as steadily as the soldiers were at the door.

After a final consultation, the guide announced he was ready for the attempt and moved forward, the others following. They took a roundabout way so as to reach the pagoda at the rear. They came up to the walls about half-past twelve without having met anyone; here there was no guard, nor were there windows or doors.
The night was dark. The waning moon barely cleared the horizon and was covered by heavy clouds; the height of the trees deepened the darkness.

It was not enough to reach the walls; an opening had to be made in them, and for this purpose the party had only their pocket-knives. Happily the temple walls were built of brick and wood, which could be cut through with little difficulty; once one brick had been pried out, the rest would give way easily.

They set noiselessly to work, and the Parsee on one side and Passepartout on the other began to loosen the bricks so as to make an opening two feet wide. They were getting on quickly when suddenly a cry was heard inside the temple, followed almost at once by other cries answering from outside. Passepartout and the guide stopped. Had they been heard? Was the alarm being raised? Common prudence urged them to fall back, and they did so, followed by Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis. They hid themselves in the wood again and waited until the disturbance, whatever it was, ceased, holding themselves ready to resume their attempt without delay. But, awkwardly enough, the guards now appeared at the rear of the temple and stationed themselves there, ready to prevent any surprise.

It would be difficult to describe the disappointment of the party, thus interrupted in their work. They could no longer reach the victim; how, then, could they save her? Sir Francis shook his fists, Passepartout was beside himself, and the guide gnashed his teeth with rage. The unruffled Fogg waited without betraying any emotion.
"There is nothing for us to do but go away," whispered Sir Francis.
"Nothing but go away," echoed the guide.
"Stop," said Fogg. "I am not due at Allahabad until tomorrow before noon."
"But what can you hope to do?" asked Sir Francis. "In a few hours it will be daylight, and—"
"The chance that now seems lost may turn up at the last moment."

Sir Francis would have liked to read Phileas Fogg's eyes. What was this cool Englishman thinking? Was he planning to make a rush for the young woman at the very moment of the sacrifice and boldly snatch her from her executioners?

That would be utter folly, and it was hard to believe Fogg was such a fool. Sir Francis agreed, however, to remain to the end of this terrible drama. The guide led them to the rear of the glade, where they were able to watch the sleeping groups.
Meanwhile Passepartout, who had perched himself on the lower branches of a tree, was turning over an idea that had first struck him like a flash and was now firmly lodged in his brain.

He had begun by saying to himself, "What folly!" and then repeated, "Why not, after all? It's a chance—perhaps the only one; and with such sots!" Thinking this, he slipped, with the suppleness of a serpent, down to the lowest branches, whose tips bent almost to the ground.

The hours passed, and the lighter tints in the sky now announced the approach of day, though it was not yet light. This was the moment. The slumbering crowd stirred to life, the tambourines sounded, songs and cries went up; the hour of the sacrifice had come. The doors of the pagoda swung open, and a bright light escaped from inside, in the midst of which Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis caught sight of the victim. Having shaken off the stupor of intoxication, she seemed to be struggling to escape from her executioner. Sir Francis's heart pounded; and, convulsively seizing Mr. Fogg's hand, he found an open knife in it. Just at that moment the crowd began to move. The young woman had again fallen into a stupor brought on by the fumes of hemp, and was carried among the fakirs, who escorted her with their wild religious cries.

Phileas Fogg and his companions, mingling with the rear ranks of the crowd, followed; and in two minutes they reached the banks of the stream and stopped fifty paces from the pyre, on which the rajah's corpse still lay. In the half-light they saw the victim, quite senseless, stretched out beside her husband's body. Then a torch was brought, and the wood, heavily soaked with oil, instantly caught fire.

At this moment Sir Francis and the guide seized Phileas Fogg, who, in an instant of mad generosity, was about to rush onto the pyre. But he had quickly pushed them aside when the whole scene suddenly changed. A cry of terror went up. The whole crowd threw themselves to the ground, terror-stricken.

The old rajah was not dead, then, since he rose all at once, like a spectre, took up his wife in his arms, and stepped down from the pyre in the midst of the clouds of smoke, which only heightened his ghostly appearance.
Fakirs and soldiers and priests, seized with sudden terror, lay there with their faces to the ground, not daring to lift their eyes and look upon such a prodigy.

The unconscious victim was carried along by the vigorous arms that supported her, and which she did not seem to burden in the least. Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis stood upright, the Parsee bowed his head, and Passepartout, no doubt, was scarcely less stupefied.
The resurrected rajah approached Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg, and, in an abrupt tone, said, "Let us be off!"

It was Passepartout himself, who had slipped onto the pyre in the midst of the smoke and, taking advantage of the darkness that still hung over them, had delivered the young woman from death! It was Passepartout who, playing his part with a fortunate boldness, had passed through the crowd in the midst of the general terror.

A moment later all four of the party had vanished into the woods, and the elephant was bearing them away at a rapid pace. But the cries and noise, and a ball that whizzed through Phileas Fogg's hat, told them the trick had been discovered.

The old rajah's body did, indeed, now appear on the burning pyre; and the priests, recovering from their terror, realized that an abduction had taken place. They rushed into the forest, followed by the soldiers, who fired a volley after the fugitives; but the latter quickly increased the distance between them, and before long found themselves out of reach of bullets and arrows.

chapters.title: Chapter 14. In which Phileas Fogg Descends the Whole Length of the Beautiful Valley of the Ganges Without Ever Thinking of Seeing It
paragraphs: The rash exploit had been carried off; and for an hour Passepartout laughed cheerfully at his success. Sir Francis pressed the worthy fellow's hand, and his master said, "Well done!"—which, from him, was high praise. To which Passepartout replied that all the credit of the affair belonged to Mr. Fogg. As for himself, he had only been struck with a "queer" idea; and he laughed to think that for a few moments he, Passepartout, the ex-gymnast and ex-sergeant fireman, had been the spouse of a charming woman—a venerable, embalmed rajah! As for the young Indian woman, she had been unconscious all through what had passed, and now, wrapped in a travelling-blanket, was resting in one of the howdahs.

The elephant, thanks to the skillful guidance of the Parsee, was moving quickly through the still-dim forest, and an hour after leaving the pagoda had crossed a vast plain. They halted at seven o'clock, the young woman still in a state of complete prostration. The guide made her drink a little brandy and water, but the drowsiness that stupefied her could not yet be shaken off. Sir Francis, who knew the effects of the intoxication produced by the fumes of hemp, reassured his companions about her. But he was more worried about her future fate. He told Phileas Fogg that if Aouda remained in India, she would inevitably fall back into the hands of her executioners. These fanatics were scattered throughout the county, and, despite the English police, they would recover their victim at Madras, Bombay, or Calcutta. She would only be safe by leaving India forever.
Phileas Fogg replied that he would think the matter over.

The station at Allahabad was reached about ten o'clock, and the interrupted line of railway, now resumed, would let them reach Calcutta in less than twenty-four hours. Phileas Fogg would thus be able to arrive in time to catch the steamer that left Calcutta the next day, October 25th, at noon for Hong Kong.

The young woman was placed in one of the waiting rooms of the station, while Passepartout was charged with buying for her various articles of toilet—a dress, a shawl, and some furs; for which his master gave him unlimited credit. Passepartout set off at once and found himself in the streets of Allahabad—that is, the City of God, one of the most venerated in India, built at the junction of the two sacred rivers, the Ganges and the Jumna, whose waters draw pilgrims from every part of the peninsula. The Ganges, according to the legends of the Ramayana, rises in heaven, from which, through Brahma's agency, it descends to the earth.

Passepartout made a point, as he made his purchases, of taking a good look at the city. It had once been defended by a noble fort, which has since become a state prison; its commerce has dwindled, and Passepartout looked around in vain for the kind of bazaar he used to frequent in Regent Street. At last he came upon an elderly, crusty Jew, a dealer in second-hand articles, from whom he bought a dress of Scotch stuff, a large mantle, and a fine otter-skin pelisse, for which he did not hesitate to pay seventy-five pounds. He then returned triumphantly to the station.
The influence to which the priests of Pillaji had subjected Aouda began gradually to wear off, and she became more herself, so that her fine eyes recovered all their soft Indian expression.
When the poet-king Ucaf Uddaul celebrates the charms of the queen of Ahmehnagara, he speaks like this:

"Her shining tresses, divided in two parts, encircle the harmonious contour of her white and delicate cheeks, brilliant in their glow and freshness. Her ebony brows have the form and charm of the bow of Kama, the god of love, and beneath her long silken lashes the purest reflections and a celestial light swim, as in the sacred lakes of Himalaya, in the black pupils of her great clear eyes. Her teeth, fine, even, and white, glitter between her smiling lips like dewdrops in a passion-flower's half-enveloped breast. Her delicately formed ears, her vermilion hands, her little feet, curved and tender as the lotus-bud, glitter with the brilliancy of the loveliest pearls of Ceylon, the most dazzling diamonds of Golconda. Her narrow and supple waist, which a hand may clasp around, sets forth the outline of her rounded figure and the beauty of her bosom, where youth in its flower displays the wealth of its treasures; and beneath the silken folds of her tunic she seems to have been modelled in pure silver by the godlike hand of Vicvarcarma, the immortal sculptor."

It is enough to say, without applying this poetic rhapsody to Aouda, that she was a charming woman in every European sense of the phrase. She spoke English with great purity, and the guide had not exaggerated in saying that the young Parsee had been transformed by her upbringing.

The train was about to leave Allahabad, and Mr. Fogg proceeded to pay the guide the price agreed upon for his service, and not a farthing more—which astonished Passepartout, who remembered all that his master owed to the guide's devotion. The Parsee had, in fact, risked his life in the adventure at Pillaji, and if he were caught later by the Indians, he would hardly escape their vengeance. Kiouni, too, had to be dealt with. What was to be done with the elephant, who had been so dearly bought? Phileas Fogg had already settled this question.
"Parsee," he said to the guide, "you have been helpful and devoted. I have paid you for your service, but not for your devotion. Would you like to have this elephant? He is yours."
The guide's eyes glistened.
"Your honour is giving me a fortune!" he cried.
"Take him, guide," returned Mr. Fogg, "and I shall still be your debtor."
"Good!" exclaimed Passepartout. "Take him, friend. Kiouni is a brave and faithful beast." And, going up to the elephant, he gave him several lumps of sugar, saying, "Here, Kiouni, here, here."

The elephant grunted out his satisfaction and, clasping Passepartout around the waist with his trunk, lifted him as high as his head. Passepartout, not in the least alarmed, stroked the animal, which gently set him down on the ground.

Soon after, Phileas Fogg, Sir Francis Cromarty, and Passepartout, settled in a carriage with Aouda, who had the best seat, were tearing along at full speed toward Benares. It was a run of eighty miles, covered in two hours. During the journey the young woman fully recovered her senses. How astonished she was to find herself in this carriage, on the railway, dressed in European clothes, and with travelers who were complete strangers to her! Her companions first set about reviving her fully with a little liquor, and then Sir Francis told her what had happened, dwelling on the courage with which Phileas Fogg had not hesitated to risk his life to save her, and recounting the happy outcome of the venture—the result of Passepartout's rash idea. Mr. Fogg said nothing, while Passepartout, embarrassed, kept repeating that "it wasn't worth telling."

Aouda pathetically thanked her deliverers, more with tears than with words; her fine eyes spoke her gratitude better than her lips. Then, as her thoughts drifted back to the scene of the sacrifice and recalled the dangers that still threatened her, she shuddered with terror.

Phileas Fogg understood what was going on in Aouda's mind, and offered, in order to reassure her, to escort her to Hong Kong, where she might remain safely until the affair was hushed up—an offer which she eagerly and gratefully accepted. She had, it appeared, a Parsee relation who was one of the leading merchants of Hong Kong, which is entirely an English city, though on an island off the Chinese coast.

At half-past twelve the train stopped at Benares. The Brahmin legends maintain that this city is built on the site of the ancient Casi, which, like Mahomet's tomb, once hung suspended between heaven and earth; though the Benares of today, which the Orientalists call the Athens of India, stands quite unpoetically on solid ground. Passepartout caught glimpses of its brick houses and clay huts, giving the place a desolate look as the train entered it.

Benares was Sir Francis Cromarty's destination, the troops he was rejoining being encamped some miles north of the city. He bade farewell to Phileas Fogg, wishing him every success, and expressing the hope that he would come that way again in a less original but more profitable fashion. Mr. Fogg lightly pressed him by the hand. Aouda's parting, who did not forget what she owed to Sir Francis, was warmer; and, as for Passepartout, he received a hearty handshake from the gallant general.

The railway, on leaving Benares, ran for a while along the valley of the Ganges. Through the windows of their carriage the travelers caught glimpses of the varied landscape of Behar, with its mountains clothed in green, its fields of barley, wheat, and corn, its jungles peopled with green alligators, its neat villages, and its still thickly-leaved forests. Elephants were bathing in the waters of the sacred river, and groups of Indians, despite the late season and the chilly air, were solemnly performing their pious ablutions. These were fervent Brahmins, the bitterest foes of Buddhism—their deities being Vishnu, the solar god, Shiva, the divine impersonation of natural forces, and Brahma, the supreme ruler of priests and legislators. What would these divinities think of India, anglicised as it is today, with steamers whistling and scudding along the Ganges, frightening the gulls floating on its surface, the turtles swarming along its banks, and the faithful living along its shores?

The panorama swept past their eyes like a flash, except when the steam fitfully hid it from view; the travelers could scarcely make out the fort of Chupenie, twenty miles south-west of Benares, the ancient stronghold of the rajahs of Behar; or Ghazipur and its famous rose-water factories; or the tomb of Lord Cornwallis, rising on the left bank of the Ganges; the fortified town of Buxar, or Patna, a large manufacturing and trading place, where the principal opium market of India is held; or Monghir, a more than European town, for it is as English as Manchester or Birmingham, with its iron foundries, edge-tool factories, and high chimneys puffing clouds of black smoke heavenward.

Night came on; the train rushed on at full speed, in the midst of the roaring of the tigers, bears, and wolves that fled before the locomotive; and the marvels of Bengal—Golconda, ruined Gour, Murshedabad the ancient capital, Burdwan, Hugly, and the French town of Chandernagor, where Passepartout would have been proud to see his country's flag flying—were hidden from their view in the darkness.
Calcutta was reached at seven in the morning, and the packet left for Hong Kong at noon; so Phileas Fogg had five hours before him.

According to his journal he was due in Calcutta on the 25th of October, and that was the exact date of his actual arrival. He was therefore neither behind time nor ahead of it. The two days gained between London and Bombay had been lost, as we have seen, on the journey across India. But it is not to be supposed that Phileas Fogg regretted them.

chapters.title: Chapter 15. In which the Bag of Banknotes Disgorges Some Thousands of Pounds More
paragraphs: The train pulled into the station, and Passepartout, jumping out first, was followed by Mr. Fogg, who helped his fair companion down. Phileas Fogg meant to head straight to the Hong Kong steamer in order to get Aouda comfortably settled for the voyage. He was unwilling to leave her while they were still on dangerous ground.
Just as he was leaving the station, a policeman came up to him and said, "Mr. Phileas Fogg?"
"I am he."
"Is this man your servant?" added the policeman, pointing to Passepartout.
"Yes."
"Be so good, both of you, as to follow me."

Mr. Fogg showed no surprise whatever. The policeman was a representative of the law, and law is sacred to an Englishman. Passepartout tried to argue the matter, but the policeman tapped him with his stick, and Mr. Fogg signaled him to obey.
"May this young lady go with us?" he asked.
"She may," replied the policeman.

Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout were conducted to a palkigahri, a sort of four-wheeled carriage drawn by two horses, in which they took their places and were driven off. No one spoke during the twenty minutes that passed before they reached their destination. They first passed through the "black town," with its narrow streets, its wretched, dirty huts, and its squalid population; then through the "European town," which offered a relief in its bright brick mansions, shaded by coconut trees and bristling with masts, where, although it was early morning, elegantly dressed horsemen and handsome equipages were passing back and forth.

The carriage stopped before a modest-looking house, which, however, did not look like a private mansion. The policeman, having asked his prisoners—for so they might truly be called—to step down, led them into a room with barred windows, and said, "You will appear before Judge Obadiah at half-past eight."
He then withdrew and shut the door.
"Why, we are prisoners!" exclaimed Passepartout, dropping into a chair.
Aouda, with an emotion she tried to conceal, said to Mr. Fogg, "Sir, you must leave me to my fate! It is on my account that you are being treated this way, it is for having saved me!"

Phileas Fogg merely said that it was impossible. It was hardly likely that he would be arrested for preventing a suttee. The complainants would not dare appear with such a charge. There was some mistake. Moreover, he would not, in any event, abandon Aouda, but would escort her to Hong Kong.
"But the steamer leaves at noon!" Passepartout observed nervously.
"We shall be on board by noon," his master replied placidly.
It was said so firmly that Passepartout could not help muttering to himself, "Parbleu, that's certain! Before noon we shall be on board." But he was by no means reassured.

At half-past eight the door opened, the policeman appeared, and, asking them to follow him, led the way into an adjoining hall. It was evidently a courtroom, and a crowd of Europeans and natives already filled the back of the room.

Mr. Fogg and his two companions took their places on a bench opposite the desks of the magistrate and his clerk. Immediately afterward Judge Obadiah, a fat, round man, came in, followed by the clerk. He proceeded to take down a wig that was hanging on a nail and put it hurriedly on his head.
"The first case," he said. Then, putting his hand to his head, he exclaimed, "Eh! This is not my wig!"
"No, your worship," answered the clerk, "it is mine."
"My dear Mr. Oysterpuff, how can a judge give a wise sentence in a clerk's wig?"
The wigs were exchanged.
Passepartout was getting nervous, for the hands on the face of the big clock above the judge seemed to be moving around with terrible speed.
"The first case," repeated Judge Obadiah.
"Phileas Fogg?" called Oysterpuff.
"I am here," replied Mr. Fogg.
"Passepartout?"
"Present," responded Passepartout.
"Good," said the judge. "You have been looked for, prisoners, for two days on the trains from Bombay."
"But what are we accused of?" asked Passepartout impatiently.
"You are about to be informed."
"I am an English subject, sir," said Mr. Fogg, "and I have the right—"
"Have you been ill-treated?"
"Not at all."
"Very well; let the complainants come in."
A door was swung open by order of the judge, and three Indian priests entered.
"That's it," muttered Passepartout; "these are the rogues who were going to burn our young lady."

The priests took their places in front of the judge, and the clerk proceeded to read out, in a loud voice, a complaint of sacrilege against Phileas Fogg and his servant, who were charged with having violated a place held sacred by the Brahmin religion.
"You hear the charge?" asked the judge.
"Yes, sir," replied Mr. Fogg, consulting his watch, "and I admit it."
"You admit it?"
"I admit it, and I wish to hear these priests admit, in their turn, what they were going to do at the pagoda of Pillaji."
The priests looked at each other; they did not seem to understand what was being said.
"Yes," cried Passepartout warmly; "at the pagoda of Pillaji, where they were about to burn their victim."
The judge stared in astonishment, and the priests were stupefied.
"What victim?" said Judge Obadiah. "Burn whom? In Bombay itself?"
"Bombay?" cried Passepartout.
"Certainly. We are not speaking of the pagoda of Pillaji, but of the pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay."
"And as proof," added the clerk, "here are the desecrator's very shoes, which he left behind him."
Whereupon he set a pair of shoes down on his desk.
"My shoes!" cried Passepartout, in his surprise letting this imprudent exclamation slip out.
The confusion of master and man, who had quite forgotten the affair at Bombay for which they were now detained at Calcutta, can be imagined.

Fix the detective had foreseen the advantage Passepartout's escapade gave him, and, delaying his departure for twelve hours, had consulted the priests of Malabar Hill. Knowing that the English authorities dealt very severely with this kind of offense, he promised them a handsome sum in damages and sent them on to Calcutta by the next train. Owing to the delay caused by the rescue of the young widow, Fix and the priests reached the Indian capital before Mr. Fogg and his servant, the magistrates having already been warned by a dispatch to arrest them should they arrive. Fix's disappointment when he learned that Phileas Fogg had not turned up in Calcutta can be imagined. He made up his mind that the robber had stopped somewhere along the route and taken refuge in the southern provinces. For twenty-four hours Fix watched the station with feverish anxiety; at last he was rewarded by seeing Mr. Fogg and Passepartout arrive, accompanied by a young woman whose presence he was wholly at a loss to explain. He hurried for a policeman; and this was how the party came to be arrested and brought before Judge Obadiah.

Had Passepartout been a little less preoccupied, he would have spotted the detective tucked into a corner of the courtroom, watching the proceedings with an interest easy to understand; for the warrant had failed to reach him at Calcutta, just as it had at Bombay and Suez.
Judge Obadiah had unfortunately caught Passepartout's rash exclamation, which the poor fellow would have given the world to take back.
"The facts are admitted?" asked the judge.
"Admitted," replied Mr. Fogg coldly.

"Inasmuch," the judge went on, "as the English law protects equally and sternly the religions of the Indian people, and as the man Passepartout has admitted that he violated the sacred pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay, on the 20th of October, I condemn the said Passepartout to imprisonment for fifteen days and a fine of three hundred pounds."
"Three hundred pounds!" cried Passepartout, startled by the size of the sum.
"Silence!" shouted the constable.

"And inasmuch," the judge continued, "as it is not proved that the act was not done in connivance between the master and his servant, and as the master must in any case be held responsible for the acts of his paid servant, I condemn Phileas Fogg to a week's imprisonment and a fine of one hundred and fifty pounds."

Fix rubbed his hands softly in satisfaction; if Phileas Fogg could be detained in Calcutta a week, that would be more than enough time for the warrant to arrive. Passepartout was stupefied. This sentence ruined his master. A wager of twenty thousand pounds lost, because he, like a precious fool, had gone into that abominable pagoda!

Phileas Fogg, as self-composed as if the judgment did not concern him in the least, did not even raise his eyebrows while it was being pronounced. Just as the clerk was calling the next case, he rose and said, "I offer bail."
"You have that right," returned the judge.
Fix's blood ran cold, but he regained his composure when he heard the judge announce that the bail required for each prisoner would be one thousand pounds.
"I will pay it at once," said Mr. Fogg, taking a roll of bank-bills from the carpet-bag, which Passepartout had with him, and placing them on the clerk's desk.
"This sum will be returned to you on your release from prison," said the judge. "In the meantime, you are released on bail."
"Come!" said Phileas Fogg to his servant.
"But let them at least give me back my shoes!" cried Passepartout angrily.
"Ah, these are pretty dear shoes!" he muttered as they were handed to him. "More than a thousand pounds apiece; and besides, they pinch my feet."

Mr. Fogg, offering his arm to Aouda, then walked out, followed by the crestfallen Passepartout. Fix still nourished hopes that the robber would not, after all, leave the two thousand pounds behind him, but would decide to serve out his week in jail, and he set off on Mr. Fogg's traces. That gentleman took a carriage, and the party were soon set down on one of the quays.

The "Rangoon" was moored half a mile off in the harbor, its signal of departure hoisted at the mast-head. Eleven o'clock was striking; Mr. Fogg was an hour ahead of time. Fix saw them leave the carriage and push off in a boat for the steamer, and stamped his feet with disappointment.

"The rascal is off, after all!" he exclaimed. "Two thousand pounds sacrificed! He's as prodigal as a thief! I'll follow him to the end of the world if necessary; but at the rate he is going on, the stolen money will soon be gone."

The detective was not far wrong in this guess. Between travel expenses, bribes, the purchase of the elephant, bails, and fines, Mr. Fogg had already spent more than five thousand pounds on the way since leaving London, and the percentage of the recovered sum from the bank robber, promised to the detectives, was rapidly shrinking.

chapters.title: Chapter 16. In which Fix Does Not Seem to Understand in the Least What is Said to Him
paragraphs: The "Rangoon"—one of the Peninsular and Oriental Company's boats plying in the Chinese and Japanese seas—was a screw steamer, built of iron, weighing about seventeen hundred and seventy tons, with engines of four hundred horse-power. She was as fast, but not as well fitted out, as the "Mongolia," and Aouda was not as comfortably provided for on board as Phileas Fogg could have wished. However, the trip from Calcutta to Hong Kong was only some three thousand five hundred miles, taking from ten to twelve days, and the young woman was not difficult to please.

During the first days of the journey Aouda became better acquainted with her protector and kept giving evidence of her deep gratitude for what he had done. The phlegmatic gentleman listened to her—outwardly, at least—with coldness, neither his voice nor his manner betraying the slightest emotion; but he seemed always on the watch to make sure that nothing should be lacking for Aouda's comfort. He called on her regularly each day at certain hours, not so much to talk himself as to sit and hear her talk. He treated her with the strictest politeness, but with the precision of an automaton whose movements had been arranged for the purpose. Aouda did not quite know what to make of him, though Passepartout had given her some hints about his master's eccentricity and made her smile by telling her of the wager that was sending him round the world. After all, she owed Phileas Fogg her life, and she always saw him through the exalting medium of her gratitude.

Aouda confirmed the Parsee guide's account of her touching history. She did indeed belong to the highest of the native races of India. Many of the Parsee merchants have made great fortunes there by dealing in cotton; and one of them, Sir Jametsee Jeejeebhoy, was made a baronet by the English government. Aouda was a relative of this great man, and it was his cousin, Jeejeeh, whom she hoped to join at Hong Kong. Whether she would find a protector in him she could not say; but Mr. Fogg tried to calm her anxieties and assure her that everything would be mathematically—he used the very word—arranged. Aouda fastened her great eyes, "clear as the sacred lakes of the Himalaya," upon him; but the intractable Fogg, as reserved as ever, did not seem at all inclined to throw himself into this lake.

The first few days of the voyage passed prosperously, amid favorable weather and propitious winds, and they soon came in sight of the great Andaman, the principal island in the Bay of Bengal, with its picturesque Saddle Peak, two thousand four hundred feet high, looming above the waters. The steamer passed close to the shores, but the savage Papuans, who are at the lowest scale of humanity, but are not, as has been claimed, cannibals, did not make their appearance.

The panorama of the islands, as they steamed by them, was superb. Vast forests of palms, arecs, bamboo, teakwood, of the gigantic mimosa and tree-like ferns, covered the foreground, while behind them the graceful outlines of the mountains were traced against the sky; and along the coasts swarmed by the thousands the precious swallows whose nests furnish a luxurious dish for the tables of the Celestial Empire. The varied landscape offered by the Andaman Islands was soon left behind, however, and the "Rangoon" was rapidly nearing the Straits of Malacca, which gave access to the China seas.

What was detective Fix, so unluckily drawn on from country to country, doing all this time? He had managed to embark on the "Rangoon" at Calcutta without being seen by Passepartout, after leaving orders that if the warrant should arrive, it should be forwarded to him at Hong Kong; and he hoped to keep his presence concealed to the end of the voyage. It would have been difficult to explain why he was on board without rousing Passepartout's suspicions, since Passepartout believed he was still at Bombay. But necessity drove him, nevertheless, to renew his acquaintance with the worthy servant, as will be seen.

All the detective's hopes and wishes now centered on Hong Kong; for the steamer's stay at Singapore would be too brief to allow him to take any steps there. The arrest must be made at Hong Kong, or the robber would probably escape him forever. Hong Kong was the last English ground on which he would set foot; beyond it, China, Japan, and America offered Fogg an almost certain refuge. If the warrant should at last turn up at Hong Kong, Fix could arrest him and hand him over to the local police, and there would be no further trouble. But beyond Hong Kong, a simple warrant would be of no use; an extradition warrant would be needed, and that would mean delays and obstacles of which the rascal would take advantage to slip away from justice.

Fix turned these probabilities over in his mind during the long hours he spent in his cabin, and kept repeating to himself, "Now, either the warrant will be at Hong Kong, in which case I shall arrest my man, or it will not be there; and this time it is absolutely necessary that I delay his departure. I have failed at Bombay, and I have failed at Calcutta; if I fail at Hong Kong, my reputation is lost. Cost what it may, I _must_ succeed! But how shall I prevent his departure, if that should turn out to be my last resource?"

Fix made up his mind that, if the worst came to the worst, he would take Passepartout into his confidence and tell him what kind of fellow his master really was. That Passepartout was not Fogg's accomplice he was quite sure. The servant, enlightened by his disclosure and afraid of being himself implicated in the crime, would no doubt become an ally of the detective. But this method was a dangerous one, only to be used when everything else had failed. A single word from Passepartout to his master would ruin everything. The detective was therefore in a tight spot. But suddenly a new idea struck him. The presence of Aouda on the "Rangoon," in the company of Phileas Fogg, gave him new material for reflection.

Who was this woman? What combination of events had made her Fogg's traveling companion? They had evidently met somewhere between Bombay and Calcutta; but where? Had they met by chance, or had Fogg gone into the interior on purpose in quest of this charming damsel? Fix was fairly puzzled. He asked himself whether there had not been a wicked elopement; and this idea so impressed itself upon his mind that he determined to make use of the supposed intrigue. Whether the young woman were married or not, he would be able to create such difficulties for Mr. Fogg at Hong Kong that he could not escape by paying any amount of money.
But could he even wait until they reached Hong Kong? Fogg had an abominable way of jumping from one boat to another, and before anything could be done he might be fully under way again for Yokohama.

Fix decided he must warn the English authorities and signal the "Rangoon" before her arrival. This was easy to do, since the steamer stopped at Singapore, from which there is a telegraph wire to Hong Kong. Moreover, before acting more decisively, he finally resolved to question Passepartout. It would not be hard to make him talk; and, as there was no time to lose, Fix prepared to make himself known.
It was now the 30th of October, and on the following day the "Rangoon" was due at Singapore.

Fix came out of his cabin and went on deck. Passepartout was strolling up and down in the forward part of the steamer. The detective rushed forward with every appearance of extreme surprise, and exclaimed, "You here, on the 'Rangoon'?"

"What, Monsieur Fix, are you on board?" replied the genuinely astonished Passepartout, recognizing his crony of the "Mongolia." "Why, I left you at Bombay, and here you are, on the way to Hong Kong! Are you going round the world too?"
"No, no," replied Fix; "I shall stop at Hong Kong—at least for some days."
"Hum!" said Passepartout, who seemed for an instant perplexed. "But how is it I haven't seen you on board since we left Calcutta?"
"Oh, a trifle of seasickness—I've been staying in my berth. The Gulf of Bengal doesn't agree with me as well as the Indian Ocean. And how is Mr. Fogg?"
"As well and as punctual as ever, not a day behind time! But, Monsieur Fix, you don't know that we have a young lady with us."
"A young lady?" replied the detective, not seeming to understand what was said.

Passepartout thereupon recounted Aouda's history—the affair at the Bombay pagoda, the purchase of the elephant for two thousand pounds, the rescue, the arrest, and the sentence of the Calcutta court, and the release of Mr. Fogg and himself on bail. Fix, who was familiar with the latter events, seemed equally ignorant of everything Passepartout related; and the latter was charmed to find so interested a listener.
"But does your master mean to take this young woman to Europe?"
"Not at all. We are simply going to place her under the protection of one of her relatives, a rich merchant at Hong Kong."
"Nothing to be done there," Fix said to himself, hiding his disappointment. "A glass of gin, Mr. Passepartout?"
"Willingly, Monsieur Fix. We must at least have a friendly glass on board the 'Rangoon.'"

chapters.title: Chapter 17. Showing What Happened on the Voyage from Singapore to Hong Kong
paragraphs: The detective and Passepartout met often on deck after this interview, though Fix was reserved and made no attempt to draw any more facts out of his companion concerning Mr. Fogg. He caught a glimpse of that mysterious gentleman once or twice; but Mr. Fogg generally kept to the cabin, where he kept Aouda company, or, by his inveterate habit, took a hand at whist.

Passepartout began very seriously to wonder what strange chance was keeping Fix still on the route his master was taking. It was really worth puzzling over: why this certainly very pleasant and obliging person, whom he had first met at Suez, had then encountered on board the "Mongolia," who disembarked at Bombay (which he announced as his destination), and now turned up so unexpectedly on the "Rangoon," was following Mr. Fogg's tracks step by step. What was Fix's object? Passepartout was ready to wager his Indian shoes—which he religiously preserved—that Fix would also leave Hong Kong at the same time as they did, and probably on the same steamer.

Passepartout might have racked his brain for a century without hitting on the real object the detective had in view. He could never have imagined that Phileas Fogg was being tracked as a robber around the globe. But, as it is in human nature to try to solve every mystery, Passepartout suddenly hit upon an explanation of Fix's movements that was, in truth, far from unreasonable. Fix, he thought, could only be an agent of Mr. Fogg's friends at the Reform Club, sent to follow him and to verify that he really was going round the world as agreed.

"It's clear!" the worthy servant repeated to himself, proud of his shrewdness. "He's a spy sent to keep us in view! That isn't quite the thing either, to be spying on Mr. Fogg, who is such an honorable man! Ah, gentlemen of the Reform Club, this shall cost you dear!"

Enchanted with his discovery, Passepartout resolved to say nothing to his master, lest he should be justly offended at this mistrust on the part of his opponents. But he decided to chaff Fix, when he had the chance, with mysterious allusions, which need not, however, betray his real suspicions.

On the afternoon of Wednesday, 30th October, the "Rangoon" entered the Strait of Malacca, which separates the peninsula of that name from Sumatra. The mountainous and craggy islets blocked the beauties of this noble island from the travelers' view. The "Rangoon" weighed anchor at Singapore the next day at four a.m. to take on coal, having gained half a day on the appointed time of her arrival. Phileas Fogg noted this gain in his journal and then, accompanied by Aouda, who showed a desire for a walk on shore, disembarked.
Fix, who suspected Mr. Fogg's every movement, followed them cautiously without being seen; while Passepartout, laughing up his sleeve at Fix's maneuvers, went about his usual errands.

The island of Singapore is not imposing in appearance, for there are no mountains; yet its look is not without charm. It is a park crossed by pleasant highways and avenues. A handsome carriage, drawn by a sleek pair of New Holland horses, carried Phileas Fogg and Aouda through rows of palms with brilliant foliage and of clove trees, whose cloves are the heart of a half-open flower. Pepper plants took the place of the prickly hedges of European fields; sago bushes and large ferns with gorgeous branches varied the look of this tropical clime; while nutmeg trees in full leaf filled the air with a penetrating perfume. Agile and grinning bands of monkeys skipped about in the trees, and tigers were not lacking in the jungles either.

After a drive of two hours through the country, Aouda and Mr. Fogg returned to the town, which is a vast collection of heavy-looking, irregular houses, surrounded by charming gardens rich in tropical fruits and plants; and at ten o'clock they re-embarked, closely followed by the detective, who had kept them constantly in sight.

Passepartout, who had been buying several dozen mangoes—a fruit as large as good-sized apples, dark-brown on the outside and a bright red within, and whose white pulp, melting in the mouth, gives gourmands a delicious sensation—was waiting for them on deck. He was only too pleased to offer some mangoes to Aouda, who thanked him very gracefully for them.

At eleven o'clock the "Rangoon" stood out of Singapore harbor, and in a few hours the high mountains of Malacca, with their forests inhabited by the most beautifully furred tigers in the world, were lost to view. Singapore is some thirteen hundred miles from the island of Hong Kong, which is a small English colony near the Chinese coast. Phileas Fogg hoped to make the trip in six days, so as to be in time for the steamer that was to leave on the 6th of November for Yokohama, the principal Japanese port.
The "Rangoon" had a large complement of passengers, many of whom disembarked at Singapore, among them a number of Indians, Ceylonese, Chinamen, Malays, and Portuguese, mostly second-class travelers.

The weather, which had so far been fine, changed with the last quarter of the moon. The sea rolled heavily, and the wind at intervals rose almost to a storm, but it happily blew from the south-west and so helped the steamer's progress. Whenever he could, the captain put up his sails, and under the double action of steam and sail the vessel made rapid progress along the coasts of Anam and Cochin China. Owing to the defective construction of the "Rangoon," however, unusual precautions became necessary in unfavorable weather; but the loss of time that resulted from this, while it nearly drove Passepartout out of his senses, did not seem to affect his master in the least. Passepartout blamed the captain, the engineer, and the crew, and consigned everyone connected with the ship to the land where the pepper grows. Perhaps the thought of the gas, which was remorselessly burning at his expense in Saville Row, had something to do with his hot impatience.
"You are in a great hurry, then," Fix said to him one day, "to reach Hong Kong?"
"A very great hurry!"
"Mr. Fogg, I suppose, is anxious to catch the steamer for Yokohama?"
"Terribly anxious."
"You believe in this journey around the world, then?"
"Absolutely. Don't you, Mr. Fix?"
"I? I don't believe a word of it."
"You're a sly dog!" said Passepartout, winking at him.

This expression rather disturbed Fix, without his knowing why. Had the Frenchman guessed his real purpose? He didn't know what to think. But how could Passepartout have found out that he was a detective? And yet, in speaking as he did, the man evidently meant more than he said.
Passepartout went still further the next day; he could not hold his tongue.
"Mr. Fix," he said in a bantering tone, "shall we be so unfortunate as to lose you when we get to Hong Kong?"
"Why," replied Fix, a little embarrassed, "I don't know; perhaps—"

"Ah, if only you would come on with us! An agent of the Peninsular Company, you know, can't stop on the way! You were only going to Bombay, and here you are in China. America isn't far off, and from America to Europe is only a step."
Fix looked intently at his companion, whose face was as serene as could be, and laughed along with him. But Passepartout went on chaffing him, asking him if he made much by his present occupation.
"Yes, and no," returned Fix; "there's good and bad luck in such things. But you must understand that I don't travel at my own expense."
"Oh, I am quite sure of that!" cried Passepartout, laughing heartily.

Fix, fairly puzzled, went down to his cabin and gave himself up to his reflections. He was evidently suspected; somehow or other the Frenchman had found out that he was a detective. But had he told his master? What part was he playing in all this—was he an accomplice or not? Was the game, then, up? Fix spent several hours turning these things over in his mind, sometimes thinking all was lost, then persuading himself that Fogg knew nothing of his presence, and then undecided what course was best to take.

Nevertheless, he kept his coolness of mind and at last resolved to deal plainly with Passepartout. If he found it impractical to arrest Fogg at Hong Kong, and if Fogg made preparations to leave that last foothold of English territory, then he, Fix, would tell Passepartout everything. Either the servant was his master's accomplice—in which case the master knew of his operations and he would fail—or else the servant knew nothing about the robbery, in which case his interest would lie in abandoning the robber.

Such was the situation between Fix and Passepartout. Meanwhile Phileas Fogg moved above them in the most majestic and unconscious indifference. He was passing methodically in his orbit around the world, indifferent to the lesser stars that gravitated around him. And yet there was nearby what the astronomers would call a disturbing star, which might have produced an agitation in this gentleman's heart. But no! the charms of Aouda failed to act, to Passepartout's great surprise; and the disturbances, if any existed, would have been harder to calculate than those of Uranus that led to the discovery of Neptune.

It was an ever-growing wonder to Passepartout, who read in Aouda's eyes the depths of her gratitude to his master. Phileas Fogg, though brave and gallant, must, he thought, be quite heartless. As for any sentiment that this journey might have awakened in him, there was clearly no trace of such a thing; while poor Passepartout lived in perpetual daydreams.

One day he was leaning on the railing of the engine-room and watching the engine when a sudden pitch of the steamer threw the screw out of the water. The steam came hissing out of the valves; and this made Passepartout indignant.
"The valves are not sufficiently charged!" he exclaimed. "We're not going. Oh, these English! If this were an American craft, we might blow up, perhaps, but at all events we would go faster!"

chapters.title: Chapter 18. In which Phileas Fogg, Passepartout, and Fix Go each about His Business
paragraphs: The weather was bad during the latter days of the voyage. The wind, obstinately holding in the north-west, blew a gale and held the steamer back. The "Rangoon" rolled heavily, and the passengers grew impatient with the long, monstrous waves that the wind raised across their path. A sort of tempest came up on the 3rd of November, the squall knocking the vessel about with fury and the waves running high. The "Rangoon" reefed all her sails, and even the rigging proved too much, whistling and shaking amid the squall. The steamer was forced to move slowly, and the captain estimated that she would reach Hong Kong twenty hours behind time, and more if the storm lasted.

Phileas Fogg gazed at the tempestuous sea—which seemed to be struggling especially to delay him—with his habitual tranquility. He never changed countenance for an instant, though a delay of twenty hours, by making him too late for the Yokohama boat, would almost inevitably mean the loss of the wager. But this man of nerve showed neither impatience nor annoyance; it was as if the storm were a part of his program and had been foreseen. Aouda was amazed to find him as calm as he had been from the first time she saw him.

Fix did not view the state of things in the same light. The storm pleased him greatly. His satisfaction would have been complete had the "Rangoon" been forced to retreat before the violence of wind and waves. Each delay filled him with hope, for it was becoming more and more probable that Fogg would have to remain some days at Hong Kong; and now the heavens themselves became his allies, with the gusts and squalls. It did not matter that they made him seasick—he took no account of this inconvenience; and, while his body was writhing under their effects, his spirit bounded with hopeful exultation.

Passepartout was enraged beyond words by the unpropitious weather. Everything had gone so well till now! Earth and sea had seemed to be at his master's service; steamers and railways obeyed him; wind and steam combined to speed his journey. Had the hour of adversity come? Passepartout was as worked up as if the twenty thousand pounds were to come out of his own pocket. The storm exasperated him, the gale made him furious, and he longed to lash the stubborn sea into obedience. Poor fellow! Fix carefully concealed his own satisfaction from him, for, had he betrayed it, Passepartout could scarcely have kept himself from personal violence.

Passepartout stayed on deck as long as the tempest lasted, unable to stay quiet below, and taking it into his head to help the ship along by lending a hand with the crew. He overwhelmed the captain, officers, and sailors—who could not help laughing at his impatience—with all sorts of questions. He wanted to know exactly how long the storm was going to last; whereupon he was referred to the barometer, which seemed to have no intention of rising. Passepartout shook it, but with no perceptible effect; for neither shaking nor maledictions could prevail on it to change its mind.

On the 4th, however, the sea grew calmer and the storm let up in violence; the wind veered to the south and was once more favorable. Passepartout cleared up with the weather. Some of the sails were unfurled, and the "Rangoon" resumed its most rapid speed. The time lost could not, however, be made up. Land was not sighted until five o'clock on the morning of the 6th; the steamer was due on the 5th. Phileas Fogg was twenty-four hours behind, and the Yokohama steamer would, of course, be missed.

The pilot came on board at six and took his place on the bridge to guide the "Rangoon" through the channels into the port of Hong Kong. Passepartout longed to ask him whether the steamer had left for Yokohama; but he dared not, for he wished to preserve the spark of hope that still remained till the last moment. He had confided his anxiety to Fix, who—the sly rascal!—tried to console him by saying that Mr. Fogg would be in time if he took the next boat; but this only put Passepartout in a passion.
Mr. Fogg, bolder than his servant, did not hesitate to approach the pilot and tranquilly ask him if he knew when a steamer would leave Hong Kong for Yokohama.
"At high tide tomorrow morning," answered the pilot.
"Ah!" said Mr. Fogg, without betraying any astonishment.
Passepartout, who heard what was said, would willingly have embraced the pilot, while Fix would have been glad to twist his neck.
"What is the steamer's name?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"The 'Carnatic.'"
"Should she not have gone yesterday?"
"Yes, sir; but they had to repair one of her boilers, and so her departure was put off till tomorrow."
"Thank you," returned Mr. Fogg, going mathematically down to the saloon.
Passepartout clasped the pilot's hand and shook it heartily in his delight, exclaiming, "Pilot, you are the best of good fellows!"

The pilot probably does not know to this day why his answers earned him this enthusiastic greeting. He remounted the bridge and guided the steamer through the flotilla of junks, tankas, and fishing boats that crowd the harbor of Hong Kong.
At one o'clock the "Rangoon" was at the quay, and the passengers were going ashore.

Chance had strangely favored Phileas Fogg, for if the "Carnatic" had not been forced to lie over for the repair of her boilers, she would have left on the 6th of November, and the passengers for Japan would have had to wait a week for the sailing of the next steamer. Mr. Fogg was, it is true, twenty-four hours behind his time; but this could not seriously imperil the rest of his tour.

The steamer that crossed the Pacific from Yokohama to San Francisco made a direct connection with the one from Hong Kong, and could not sail until the latter reached Yokohama; and if Mr. Fogg were twenty-four hours late on reaching Yokohama, this time would no doubt be easily made up on the twenty-two-day voyage across the Pacific. So he found himself about twenty-four hours behind time, thirty-five days after leaving London.

The "Carnatic" was announced to leave Hong Kong at five the next morning. Mr. Fogg had sixteen hours in which to attend to his business there, which was to deposit Aouda safely with her wealthy relative.

On landing, he conducted her to a palanquin, in which they made their way to the Club Hotel. A room was engaged for the young woman, and Mr. Fogg, after seeing that she wanted for nothing, set out in search of her cousin Jeejeeh. He instructed Passepartout to remain at the hotel until his return, so that Aouda would not be left entirely alone.

Mr. Fogg went to the Exchange, where, he had no doubt, everyone would know so wealthy and considerable a personage as the Parsee merchant.
