Han indledte varme venskaber med sømændene og forbløffede dem med sine akrobatiske kunststykker. Han mente, de håndterede skibet som gentlemen, og at fyrbøderne fyrede som helte. Hans snakkesalige godt humør smittede alle. Han havde glemt fortiden, dens ærgrelser og dens forsinkelser. Han tænkte kun på målet, der nu lå så nær; og undertiden kogte han over af utålmodighed, som om han var ophedet af »Henrietta«s fyrkedler. Ofte gik den brave karl også rundt om Fix og betragtede ham med et skarpt, mistroisk blik; men han talte ikke til ham, for deres gamle fortrolighed var forbi.

Fix, må man indrømme, forstod intet af, hvad der foregik. Erobringen af »Henrietta«, bestikkelsen af besætningen, Fogg, der håndterede båden som en kyndig sømand — alt forbløffede og forvirrede ham. Han vidste ikke, hvad han skulle tænke. Når alt kom til alt, kunne en mand, der begyndte med at stjæle femoghalvtreds tusind pund, godt ende med at stjæle et fartøj; og Fix var ikke unaturligt tilbøjelig til at slutte, at »Henrietta« under Foggs kommando slet ikke var på vej til Liverpool, men til en eller anden del af verden, hvor røveren — nu sørøver — i fred kunne bringe sig selv i sikkerhed. Antagelsen var i det mindste plausibel, og detektiven begyndte for alvor at fortryde, at han havde indladt sig på sagen.

Hvad kaptajn Speedy angik, fortsatte han med at hyle og knurre i sin kahyt; og Passepartout, hvis pligt det var at bringe ham hans måltider, modig som han var, tog de største forsigtighedsregler. Mr. Fogg syntes end ikke at vide, at der var en kaptajn om bord.

Den 13. passerede de kanten af Newfoundlandbankerne, en farlig strækning; især om vinteren er der hyppige tåger og kraftige stormvinde. Lige siden aftenen før havde barometeret, der pludselig var faldet, varslet et kommende vejrskifte; og om natten skiftede temperaturen, kulden skærpedes, og vinden drejede mod sydøst.

Det var et uheld. For ikke at afvige fra sin kurs rebede Mr. Fogg sejlene og øgede dampen; men fartøjets fart slappede på grund af søens tilstand, hvis lange bølger brækkede mod dens hæk. Det huggede voldsomt, og dette sinkede dets fremgang. Lidt efter lidt voksede brisen til en storm, og det var at frygte, at »Henrietta« ikke ville kunne holde sig oprejst på bølgerne.

Passepartouts ansigt mørknede sammen med himlen, og i to dage levede den stakkels fyr i bestandig angst. Men Phileas Fogg var en dristig sømand og forstod at holde fart mod søen; han holdt sin kurs uden engang at slække dampen. Når »Henrietta« ikke kunne rejse sig over bølgerne, krydsede den igennem dem og oversvømmede dækket, men kom velbeholden igennem. Undertiden løftede skruen sig ud af vandet og slog sin blottede ende, når et bjerg af vand hævede hækken over bølgerne; men fartøjet holdt altid lige ud.

Vinden voksede dog ikke så voldsomt, som man havde kunnet frygte; det var ikke en af de storme, der bryder ud og styrter af sted med en hastighed af halvfems miles i timen. Den forblev frisk, men forblev desværre stædigt i sydøst og gjorde sejlene ubrugelige.

Den 16. december var den femoghalvfjerdsindstyvende dag siden Phileas Foggs afrejse fra London, og »Henrietta« var endnu ikke blevet alvorligt forsinket. Halvdelen af rejsen var næsten fuldført, og de værste strækninger var passeret. Om sommeren ville sejren have været så godt som sikker. Om vinteren var de prisgivet den dårlige årstid. Passepartout sagde intet; men han nærede i hemmelighed sit håb og trøstede sig med tanken om, at hvis vinden svigtede dem, kunne de stadig regne med dampen.

På denne dag kom maskinmesteren op på dækket, gik hen til Mr. Fogg og begyndte at tale alvorligt med ham. Uden at vide hvorfor — måske en anelse — blev Passepartout vagt urolig. Han ville have givet det ene øre for at høre med det andet, hvad maskinmesteren sagde. Det lykkedes ham til sidst at opfange nogle få ord, og han var sikker på at have hørt sin herre sige: »De er sikker på, hvad De fortæller mig?«

»Sikker, sir,« svarede maskinmesteren. »De må huske, at vi siden afgangen har holdt varme ild i alle vore fyr, og at vi — selv om vi havde kul nok til at sejle med lav damp fra New York til Bordeaux — ikke har nok til at sejle med fuld damp fra New York til Liverpool.« »Jeg vil overveje det,« svarede Mr. Fogg.

Passepartout opfattede alt; han blev grebet af dødelig angst. Kullene var ved at slippe op! »Ah, hvis min herre kan komme over det,« mumlede han, »vil han være en berømt mand!« Han kunne ikke lade være med at viderebringe til Fix, hvad han havde hørt.
»Så De tror virkelig, vi sejler til Liverpool?«
»Naturligvis.«
»Æsel!« svarede detektiven, trak på skuldrene og drejede om på hælen.

Passepartout var på nippet til kraftigt at protestere mod tilnavnet, hvis grund han ikke for sit bare liv kunne forstå; men han overvejede, at den ulykkelige Fix sandsynligvis var meget skuffet og ydmyget i sin selvfølelse efter så kejtet at have fulgt et falsk spor rundt om jorden, og lod det passere.

Og hvad kurs ville Phileas Fogg nu tage? Det var svært at forestille sig. Dog syntes han at have besluttet sig for én, for samme aften sendte han bud efter maskinmesteren og sagde til ham: »Fyr alle ild op, indtil kullet er opbrugt.«

Få øjeblikke senere spyede »Henrietta«s skorsten skyer af røg ud. Fartøjet fortsatte med fuld damp; men den 18. meddelte maskinmesteren — som han havde forudsagt — at kullene ville slippe op i løbet af dagen.
»Lad ikke ildene gå ned,« svarede Mr. Fogg. »Hold dem oppe til det sidste. Lad ventilerne være fyldte.«

Henimod middag kaldte Phileas Fogg — efter at have fastslået deres position — på Passepartout og bød ham hente kaptajn Speedy. Det var, som om den ærlige fyr var blevet bedt om at slippe en tiger løs. Han gik op til hytten og sagde til sig selv: »Han bliver som en gal mand!«

Få minutter senere viste der sig midt i råb og eder en bombe på hytten. Bomben var kaptajn Speedy. Det var tydeligt, at han var på nippet til at sprænges. »Hvor er vi?« var de første ord, hans vrede tillod ham at udstøde. Havde den stakkels mand været tilbøjelig til apopleksi, ville han aldrig være kommet sig over sit anfald af raseri.
»Hvor er vi?« gentog han, mens hans ansigt blev purpurrødt.
»Syv hundrede og syv miles fra Liverpool,« svarede Mr. Fogg med uforstyrrelig ro.
»Pirat!« råbte kaptajn Speedy.
»Jeg har sendt bud efter Dem, sir —«
»Røverpak!«
»— sir,« fortsatte Mr. Fogg, »for at bede Dem sælge mig Deres fartøj.«
»Nej! Ved alle djævle, nej!«
»Men jeg vil blive nødt til at brænde det.«
»Brænde »Henrietta«!«
»Ja, i det mindste den øverste del af det. Kullene er sluppet op.«
»Brænde mit fartøj!« råbte kaptajn Speedy, der knap kunne få ordene frem. »Et fartøj til halvtreds tusind dollars!«

»Her er tres tusind,« svarede Phileas Fogg og rakte kaptajnen en rulle pengesedler. Dette havde en uhyre virkning på Andrew Speedy. En amerikaner kan næppe forholde sig upåvirket ved synet af tres tusind dollars. Kaptajnen glemte i et øjeblik sin vrede, sin fangenskab og alle sine nag mod sin passager. »Henrietta« var tyve år gammel; det var et særdeles godt køb. Bomben ville alligevel ikke gå af. Mr. Fogg havde fjernet lunten.
»Og jeg vil stadig have jernskroget,« sagde kaptajnen i en mildere tone.
»Jernskroget og maskinen. Er det aftalt?«
»Aftalt.«
Og Andrew Speedy greb pengesedlerne, talte dem og puttede dem i lommen.

Under denne udveksling var Passepartout hvid som et lagen, og Fix så ud, som om han var på nippet til at få et apoplektisk anfald. Næsten tyve tusind pund var brugt, og Fogg overlod skroget og maskinen til kaptajnen — det vil sige næsten hele fartøjets værdi! Sandt nok var dog, at femoghalvtreds tusind pund var stjålet fra Bank of England.

Da Andrew Speedy havde stukket pengene i lommen, sagde Mr. Fogg til ham: »Lad ikke dette forbavse Dem, sir. De skal vide, at jeg vil tabe tyve tusind pund, medmindre jeg når London inden kvart i ni om aftenen den 21. december. Jeg gik glip af damperen i New York, og da De nægtede at føre mig til Liverpool —«
»Og det gjorde jeg klogt i!« råbte Andrew Speedy. »For jeg har tjent mindst fyrre tusind dollars på det!« Han tilføjede mere besindigt: »Ved De én ting, kaptajn —«
»Fogg.«
»Kaptajn Fogg, De har noget af yankeen i Dem.«
Og efter at have aflagt sin passager, hvad han betragtede som en stor kompliment, var han ved at vende sig om for at gå, da Mr. Fogg sagde: »Fartøjet tilhører altså mig nu?«
»Vist så — fra køl til mastetop, alt træværket, vel at mærke.«
»Godt. Få de indvendige sæder, køjer og rammer revet ned, og brænd dem.«

Det var nødvendigt at have tørt træ for at holde dampen oppe på det krævede tryk, og den dag blev hytten, kahytterne, køjerne og reservedækket ofret. Den næste dag, den 19. december, blev masterne, rærne og bommene brændt; besætningen arbejdede med liv og lyst og holdt ildene oppe. Passepartout huggede, skar og savede af alle kræfter. Der var et formeligt raseri for nedrivning.

Rælingerne, beslagene, det meste af dækket og overbordene forsvandt den 20., og »Henrietta« var nu kun en flad pram. Men på den dag fik de øje på Irlands kyst og Fastnet Light. Klokken ti om aftenen passerede de Queenstown. Phileas Fogg havde kun fireogtyve timer tilbage til at nå London; det var den tid, der krævedes for at nå Liverpool med fuld damp. Og dampen var lige ved at slippe helt op!
»Sir,« sagde kaptajn Speedy, der nu var dybt interesseret i Mr. Foggs forehavende, »det gør mig virkelig ondt for Dem. Alt er imod Dem. Vi er kun ud for Queenstown.«
»Ah,« sagde Mr. Fogg, »er det sted, hvor vi ser lysene, Queenstown?«
»Ja.«
»Kan vi løbe ind i havnen?«
»Ikke i tre timer endnu. Kun ved højvande.«
»Vi venter,« svarede Mr. Fogg roligt, uden at lade det vise sig på sit ansigt, at han ved en suveræn indskydelse var i færd med endnu en gang at forsøge at overvinde uheldet.

Queenstown er den irske havn, hvor de transatlantiske dampere standser for at sætte posten af. Denne post føres til Dublin af ekspressetog, som altid holder klar til at afgå; fra Dublin sendes den videre til Liverpool med de hurtigste både og vinder dermed tolv timer på Atlanterhavsdamperne.

Phileas Fogg regnede med at vinde tolv timer på samme måde. I stedet for at ankomme til Liverpool næste aften med »Henrietta« ville han være der ved middagstid og derved have tid til at nå London inden kvart i ni om aftenen.

»Henrietta« løb ind i Queenstown havn klokken et om morgenen, da det netop var højvande; og Phileas Fogg lod, efter at kaptajn Speedy havde grebet ham hjerteligt i hånden, denne herre tilbage på sit fartøjs nivellerede pram, der stadig var halvdelen værd af, hvad han havde solgt det for.

Selskabet gik straks i land. Fix var meget fristet til at arrestere Mr. Fogg på stedet; men han gjorde det ikke. Hvorfor? Hvilken kamp foregik der i ham? Havde han skiftet mening om »sin mand«? Indså han, at han havde begået en alvorlig fejltagelse? Han forlod dog ikke Mr. Fogg. De steg alle om bord på toget, som netop var ved at afgå, klokken halv to; ved daggry var de i Dublin; og de spildte ingen tid med at gå om bord på et dampskib, der — der foragtede at hæve sig over bølgerne — uden undtagelse skar gennem dem.
Phileas Fogg gik endelig i land på kajen i Liverpool klokken tyve minutter i tolv den 21. december. Han var kun seks timer fra London.
Men i dette øjeblik trådte Fix frem, lagde sin hånd på Mr. Foggs skulder, fremviste sin arrestordre og sagde: »De er virkelig Phileas Fogg?«
»Det er jeg.«
»Jeg arresterer Dem i Dronningens navn!«

chapters.title: Chapter 34. In which Phileas Fogg at Last Reaches London
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg was in prison. He had been shut up in the Custom House, and was to be transferred to London the next day.

When Passepartout saw his master arrested, he would have fallen upon Fix had he not been held back by some policemen. Aouda was thunderstruck by the suddenness of an event she could not understand. Passepartout explained to her how it was that the honest and courageous Fogg was being arrested as a robber. The young woman’s heart revolted against so heinous a charge, and when she saw that she could attempt nothing to save her protector, she wept bitterly.
As for Fix, he had arrested Mr. Fogg because it was his duty, whether Mr. Fogg were guilty or not.

It then struck Passepartout that he was the cause of this new misfortune! Had he not concealed Fix’s errand from his master? When Fix had revealed his true character and purpose, why had he not told Mr. Fogg? If his master had been warned, he would no doubt have given Fix proof of his innocence and satisfied him of his mistake; at the very least, Fix would not have continued his journey at the expense and on the heels of his master, only to arrest him the moment he set foot on English soil. Passepartout wept till he was blind, and felt like blowing his brains out.
Aouda and he had remained, despite the cold, under the portico of the Custom House. Neither would leave the spot; both were anxious to see Mr. Fogg again.

That gentleman was indeed ruined, and ruined at the very moment when he was about to attain his goal. This arrest was fatal. Having arrived at Liverpool at twenty minutes before twelve on the 21st of December, he had until a quarter before nine that evening to reach the Reform Club—that is, nine hours and a quarter; the journey from Liverpool to London was six hours.

If anyone, at this moment, had entered the Custom House, he would have found Mr. Fogg seated, motionless, calm, and without any visible anger, on a wooden bench. He was not, it is true, resigned; but this final blow failed to force him into any outward show of emotion. Was he being devoured by one of those secret rages, all the more terrible for being held in, and which only burst forth, with an irresistible force, at the last moment? No one could tell. There he sat, calmly waiting—for what? Did he still cherish hope? Did he still believe, now that the door of this prison had closed on him, that he would succeed?

However that may have been, Mr. Fogg carefully placed his watch upon the table and watched its advancing hands. Not a word escaped his lips, but his look was singularly set and stern. The situation, in any case, was a terrible one, and could be summed up thus: if Phileas Fogg was honest, he was ruined; if he was a rogue, he was caught.

Did escape occur to him? Did he check to see if there was any practicable way out of his prison? Did he think of escaping from it? Possibly; for once he walked slowly around the room. But the door was locked and the window heavily barred with iron rods. He sat down again and drew his journal from his pocket. On the line where the words “21st December, Saturday, Liverpool” were written, he added, “80th day, 11.40 a.m.,” and waited.
The Custom House clock struck one. Mr. Fogg observed that his watch was two hours fast.
Two hours! Granting that he was at this moment taking an express train, he could reach London and the Reform Club by a quarter before nine, p.m. His forehead slightly wrinkled.

At thirty-three minutes past two he heard a singular noise outside, then a hurried opening of doors. Passepartout’s voice was audible, and immediately afterwards Fix’s. Phileas Fogg’s eyes brightened for an instant.
The door swung open, and he saw Passepartout, Aouda, and Fix, who hurried towards him.
Fix was out of breath, his hair was in disorder. He could not speak. “Sir,” he stammered, “sir—forgive me—most—unfortunate resemblance—robber arrested three days ago—you are free!”

Phileas Fogg was free! He walked to the detective, looked him steadily in the face, and, with the only rapid motion he had ever made in his life, or which he ever would make, drew back his arms and, with the precision of a machine, knocked Fix down.
“Well hit!” cried Passepartout. “Parbleu! that’s what you might call a good application of English fists!”

Fix, who found himself on the floor, did not utter a word. He had only got his deserts. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout left the Custom House without delay, got into a cab, and in a few moments stepped down at the station.

Phileas Fogg asked if there was an express train about to leave for London. It was forty minutes past two. The express train had left thirty-five minutes before. Phileas Fogg then ordered a special train.
There were several rapid locomotives on hand; but the railway arrangements did not allow the special train to leave until three o’clock.
At that hour Phileas Fogg, having spurred the engineer on with the offer of a generous reward, at last set out towards London with Aouda and his faithful servant.

It was necessary to cover the distance in five hours and a half; and this would have been easy on a clear road throughout. But there were forced delays, and when Mr. Fogg stepped down from the train at the terminus, all the clocks in London were striking ten minutes before nine.[1]
Having made the tour of the world, he was behind-hand by five minutes. He had lost the wager!
[1] A somewhat remarkable eccentricity on the part of the London clocks!—TRANSLATOR.

chapters.title: Chapter 35. In which Phileas Fogg Does Not Have to Repeat His Orders to Passepartout Twice
paragraphs: The dwellers in Saville Row would have been surprised the next day if they had been told that Phileas Fogg had returned home. His doors and windows were still closed, and no sign of any change was visible.
After leaving the station, Mr. Fogg gave Passepartout instructions to buy some provisions, and quietly went home.

He bore his misfortune with his habitual calmness. Ruined! And by the blundering of the detective! After steadily covering that long journey, overcoming a hundred obstacles, braving many dangers, and still finding time to do some good along the way, to fail near the goal by a sudden event he could not have foreseen, and against which he had no defence—it was terrible! Only a few pounds were left of the large sum he had taken with him. All that remained of his fortune was the twenty thousand pounds deposited at Barings, and that amount he owed to his friends of the Reform Club. So great had been the expense of his tour that, even if he had won, it would not have enriched him; and it is probable that he had not sought to enrich himself, being a man who laid wagers for honour’s sake rather than for the stake itself. But this wager utterly ruined him.
Mr. Fogg’s course, however, was fully decided; he knew what was left for him to do.

A room in the house in Saville Row was set aside for Aouda, who was overwhelmed with grief at her protector’s misfortune. From the words Mr. Fogg let drop, she saw that he was meditating some serious project.
Knowing that Englishmen governed by a fixed idea sometimes resort to the desperate expedient of suicide, Passepartout kept a close watch on his master, though he was careful not to let it show.

First of all, the worthy fellow had gone up to his room and put out the gas burner that had been burning for eighty days. He had found in the letter-box a bill from the gas company, and he thought it more than time to put a stop to this expense, which he had been condemned to carry.
The night passed. Mr. Fogg went to bed, but did he sleep? Aouda did not once close her eyes. Passepartout kept watch all night, like a faithful dog, at his master’s door.

Mr. Fogg called him in the morning and told him to get Aouda’s breakfast ready, and a cup of tea and a chop for himself. He asked Aouda to excuse him from breakfast and dinner, as his time would be taken up all day in putting his affairs in order. In the evening he would ask permission to have a few moments’ conversation with the young lady.

Passepartout, having received his orders, had nothing to do but carry them out. He looked at his imperturbable master, and could scarcely bring himself to leave him. His heart was full, and his conscience was tortured by remorse; for he blamed himself more bitterly than ever for being the cause of the irretrievable disaster. Yes! If he had warned Mr. Fogg, if he had betrayed Fix’s plans to him, his master would certainly not have given the detective passage to Liverpool, and then—
Passepartout could hold it in no longer.
“My master! Mr. Fogg!” he cried. “Why do you not curse me? It was my fault that—”
“I blame no one,” returned Phileas Fogg, with perfect calmness. “Go!”
Passepartout left the room and went to find Aouda, to whom he delivered his master’s message.
“Madam,” he added, “I can do nothing myself—nothing! I have no influence over my master; but you, perhaps—”

“What influence could I have?” replied Aouda. “Mr. Fogg is influenced by no one. Has he ever understood that my gratitude to him is overflowing? Has he ever read my heart? My friend, he must not be left alone for an instant! You say he is going to speak with me this evening?”
“Yes, madam; probably to arrange for your protection and comfort in England.”
“We shall see,” replied Aouda, suddenly turning pensive.

Throughout this day (Sunday) the house in Saville Row was as if uninhabited, and Phileas Fogg, for the first time since he had lived there, did not set out for his club when the Westminster clock struck half-past eleven.

Why should he present himself at the Reform? His friends no longer expected him there. Since Phileas Fogg had not appeared in the saloon the previous evening (Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine), he had lost his wager. It was not even necessary for him to go to his bankers for the twenty thousand pounds; for his opponents already had his cheque in their hands, and they had only to fill it out and send it to Barings to have the amount transferred to their credit.

Mr. Fogg, then, had no reason to go out, and so he stayed at home. He shut himself up in his room and busied himself putting his affairs in order. Passepartout was continually going up and down the stairs. The hours were long for him. He listened at his master’s door and peered through the keyhole, as if he had a perfect right to do so, and as if he feared that something terrible might happen at any moment. Sometimes he thought of Fix, but no longer with anger. Fix, like everyone else, had been mistaken about Phileas Fogg, and had only done his duty in tracking and arresting him; while he, Passepartout. . . . This thought haunted him, and he never stopped cursing his miserable folly.
Finding himself too wretched to be alone, he knocked at Aouda’s door, went into her room, sat down, without speaking, in a corner, and looked ruefully at the young woman. Aouda was still pensive.
About half-past seven in the evening Mr. Fogg sent to ask whether Aouda would receive him, and a few moments later he was alone with her.

Phileas Fogg took a chair and sat down near the fireplace, opposite Aouda. No emotion was visible on his face. The Fogg who had returned was exactly the Fogg who had gone away; there was the same calm, the same impassivity.
He sat for several minutes without speaking; then, bending his eyes on Aouda, “Madam,” he said, “will you pardon me for bringing you to England?”
“I, Mr. Fogg!” replied Aouda, checking the beating of her heart.

“Please let me finish,” returned Mr. Fogg. “When I decided to bring you far away from the country that was so unsafe for you, I was rich, and counted on putting a portion of my fortune at your disposal; then your life would have been free and happy. But now I am ruined.”
“I know it, Mr. Fogg,” replied Aouda; “and I ask you in my turn, will you forgive me for having followed you, and—who knows?—for having, perhaps, delayed you, and so contributed to your ruin?”
“Madam, you could not stay in India, and your safety could only be assured by taking you to such a distance that your persecutors could not seize you.”
“So, Mr. Fogg,” Aouda went on, “not content with rescuing me from a terrible death, you thought yourself bound to secure my comfort in a foreign land?”
“Yes, madam; but circumstances have been against me. Still, I beg to place the little I have left at your service.”
“But what will become of you, Mr. Fogg?”
“As for me, madam,” replied the gentleman coldly, “I have need of nothing.”
“But how do you look upon the fate, sir, that awaits you?”
“As I am in the habit of doing.”
“At least,” said Aouda, “want should not overtake a man like you. Your friends—”
“I have no friends, madam.”
“Your relatives—”
“I have no relatives any longer.”

“I pity you, then, Mr. Fogg, for solitude is a sad thing, with no heart in which to confide your griefs. They say, though, that misery itself, shared by two sympathetic souls, may be borne with patience.”
“They say so, madam.”
“Mr. Fogg,” said Aouda, rising and seizing his hand, “do you wish, at once, a kinswoman and a friend? Will you have me for your wife?”

Mr. Fogg, at this, rose in his turn. There was an unwonted light in his eyes, and a slight trembling of his lips. Aouda looked into his face. The sincerity, rectitude, firmness, and sweetness of this soft glance of a noble woman, who could dare all to save him to whom she owed all, at first astonished and then penetrated him. He closed his eyes for an instant, as if to escape her look. When he opened them again, “I love you!” he said, simply. “Yes, by all that is holiest, I love you, and I am entirely yours!”
“Ah!” cried Aouda, pressing his hand to her heart.
Passepartout was summoned and appeared immediately. Mr. Fogg still held Aouda’s hand in his own; Passepartout understood, and his big, round face became as radiant as the tropical sun at its zenith.
Mr. Fogg asked him if it was not too late to notify the Reverend Samuel Wilson, of Marylebone parish, that evening.
Passepartout smiled his most genial smile, and said, “Never too late.”
It was five minutes past eight.
“Will it be for tomorrow, Monday?”
“For tomorrow, Monday,” said Mr. Fogg, turning to Aouda.
“Yes; for tomorrow, Monday,” she replied.
Passepartout dashed off as fast as his legs could carry him.

chapters.title: Chapter 36. In which Phileas Fogg’s Name is Once More at a Premium on ’change
paragraphs: It is time to relate what a change took place in English public opinion when it came out that the real bank-robber, a certain James Strand, had been arrested, on the 17th of December, at Edinburgh. Three days earlier, Phileas Fogg had been a criminal whom the police were desperately hunting; now he was an honourable gentleman, mathematically pursuing his eccentric journey around the world.

The papers took up their discussion of the wager again; all those who had laid bets, for or against him, revived their interest as if by magic; the “Phileas Fogg bonds” once again became negotiable, and many new wagers were made. Phileas Fogg’s name was once more at a premium on ’Change.

His five friends of the Reform Club spent these three days in a state of feverish suspense. Would Phileas Fogg, whom they had forgotten, reappear before their eyes! Where was he at this moment? The 17th of December, the day of James Strand’s arrest, was the seventy-sixth since Phileas Fogg’s departure, and no news of him had been received. Was he dead? Had he given up the attempt, or was he still pursuing the agreed route? And would he appear on Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine in the evening, on the threshold of the Reform Club saloon?

The anxiety in which London society lived for three days cannot be described. Telegrams were sent to America and Asia for news of Phileas Fogg. Messengers were dispatched to the house in Saville Row morning and evening. No news. The police did not know what had become of the detective, Fix, who had so unfortunately followed a false trail. Bets, nevertheless, increased in number and value. Phileas Fogg, like a racehorse, was nearing his last turn. The bonds were quoted no longer at a hundred below par, but at twenty, at ten, and at five; and paralytic old Lord Albemarle even bet in his favour.

A great crowd had gathered in Pall Mall and the neighbouring streets on Saturday evening; it looked like a multitude of brokers permanently camped around the Reform Club. Circulation was impeded, and everywhere disputes, discussions, and financial transactions were going on. The police had great difficulty keeping back the crowd, and as the hour at which Phileas Fogg was due drew near, the excitement rose to its highest pitch.

The five antagonists of Phileas Fogg had met in the great saloon of the club. John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin, the bankers, Andrew Stuart, the engineer, Gauthier Ralph, the director of the Bank of England, and Thomas Flanagan, the brewer, were all waiting anxiously.
When the clock pointed to twenty minutes past eight, Andrew Stuart got up, saying, “Gentlemen, in twenty minutes the time agreed upon between Mr. Fogg and ourselves will have expired.”
“What time did the last train arrive from Liverpool?” asked Thomas Flanagan.
“At twenty-three minutes past seven,” replied Gauthier Ralph; “and the next does not arrive till ten minutes after twelve.”
“Well, gentlemen,” Andrew Stuart resumed, “if Phileas Fogg had come in the 7:23 train, he would have got here by now. We can, therefore, consider the bet as won.”

“Wait; let us not be too hasty,” replied Samuel Fallentin. “You know that Mr. Fogg is very eccentric. His punctuality is well known; he never arrives too soon, or too late; and I should not be surprised if he appeared before us at the last minute.”
“Why,” said Andrew Stuart nervously, “if I should see him, I should not believe it was he.”

“The fact is,” Thomas Flanagan resumed, “Mr. Fogg’s project was absurdly foolish. Whatever his punctuality, he could not prevent the delays that were certain to occur; and a delay of only two or three days would be fatal to his tour.”
“Observe, too,” added John Sullivan, “that we have received no word from him, even though there are telegraph lines all along his route.”

“He has lost, gentlemen,” said Andrew Stuart, “he has lost a hundred times! You know, besides, that the ‘China’—the only steamer he could have taken from New York to get here in time—arrived yesterday. I have seen a list of the passengers, and the name of Phileas Fogg is not among them. Even if we admit that fortune has favoured him, he can scarcely have reached America. I think he will be at least twenty days behind, and that Lord Albemarle will lose a cool five thousand.”
“It is clear,” replied Gauthier Ralph; “and we have nothing to do but present Mr. Fogg’s cheque at Barings tomorrow.”
At this moment, the hands of the club clock pointed to twenty minutes to nine.
“Five minutes more,” said Andrew Stuart.
The five gentlemen looked at one another. Their anxiety was becoming intense; but, not wanting to betray it, they readily accepted Mr. Fallentin’s proposal of a rubber.
“I wouldn’t give up my four thousand of the bet,” said Andrew Stuart, as he took his seat, “for three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine.”
The clock pointed to eighteen minutes to nine.
The players picked up their cards, but could not keep their eyes off the clock. Certainly, however secure they felt, minutes had never seemed so long to them!
“Seventeen minutes to nine,” said Thomas Flanagan, as he cut the cards that Ralph handed him.

Then there was a moment of silence. The great saloon was perfectly still; but the murmurs of the crowd outside could be heard, with now and then a shrill cry. The pendulum beat the seconds, which each player eagerly counted, listening, with mathematical regularity.
“Sixteen minutes to nine!” said John Sullivan, in a voice that betrayed his emotion.
One minute more, and the wager would be won. Andrew Stuart and his partners suspended their game. They laid down their cards and counted the seconds.
At the fortieth second, nothing. At the fiftieth, still nothing.
At the fifty-fifth, a loud cry was heard in the street, followed by applause, hurrahs, and some fierce growls.
The players rose from their seats.

At the fifty-seventh second the door of the saloon opened; and the pendulum had not yet beat the sixtieth second when Phileas Fogg appeared, followed by an excited crowd who had forced their way through the club doors, and in his calm voice said, “Here I am, gentlemen!”

chapters.title: Chapter 37. In which it is Shown that Phileas Fogg Gained Nothing by His Tour Around the World, Unless it Were Happiness
paragraphs: Yes; Phileas Fogg in person.

The reader will remember that at five minutes past eight in the evening—about five and twenty hours after the travellers’ arrival in London—Passepartout had been sent by his master to engage the services of the Reverend Samuel Wilson in a certain marriage ceremony that was to take place the next day.

Passepartout set off on his errand enchanted. He soon reached the clergyman’s house, but found him not at home. Passepartout waited a good twenty minutes, and when he left the reverend gentleman, it was thirty-five minutes past eight. But in what a state he was! With his hair in disorder, and no hat on his head, he ran along the street as no man was ever seen to run before, knocking down passers-by and rushing across the sidewalk like a waterspout.
In three minutes he was in Saville Row again, and staggered back into Mr. Fogg’s room.
He could not speak.
“What is the matter?” asked Mr. Fogg.
“My master!” gasped Passepartout—“marriage—impossible—”
“Impossible?”
“Impossible—for tomorrow.”
“Why so?”
“Because tomorrow—is Sunday!”
“Monday,” replied Mr. Fogg.
“No—today is Saturday.”
“Saturday? Impossible!”
“Yes, yes, yes, yes!” cried Passepartout. “You have made a mistake of one day! We arrived twenty-four hours ahead of time; but there are only ten minutes left!”
Passepartout had seized his master by the collar, and was dragging him along with irresistible force.

Phileas Fogg, thus kidnapped, without time to think, left his house, jumped into a cab, promised a hundred pounds to the cabman, and, having run over two dogs and overturned five carriages, reached the Reform Club.
The clock pointed to a quarter before nine when he appeared in the great saloon.
Phileas Fogg had accomplished the journey round the world in eighty days!
Phileas Fogg had won his wager of twenty thousand pounds!

How was it that a man so exact and fastidious could have made this error of a day? How came he to think he had arrived in London on Saturday, the twenty-first day of December, when it was really Friday, the twentieth, the seventy-ninth day only from his departure?
The cause of the error is very simple.

Phileas Fogg had, without suspecting it, gained one day on his journey, and this merely because he had travelled constantly _eastward;_ he would, on the contrary, have lost a day had he gone in the opposite direction, that is, _westward_.

In journeying eastward he had gone towards the sun, and the days therefore grew shorter for him by as many times four minutes as he crossed degrees in this direction. There are three hundred and sixty degrees on the circumference of the earth; and these three hundred and sixty degrees, multiplied by four minutes, give precisely twenty-four hours—that is, the day unconsciously gained. In other words, while Phileas Fogg, going eastward, saw the sun cross the meridian _eighty_ times, his friends in London only saw it cross the meridian _seventy-nine_ times. This is why they awaited him at the Reform Club on Saturday, and not Sunday, as Mr. Fogg supposed.
And Passepartout’s famous family watch, which had always kept London time, would have given this fact away, if only it had marked the days as well as the hours and the minutes!

Phileas Fogg, then, had won the twenty thousand pounds; but, as he had spent nearly nineteen thousand on the way, the pecuniary gain was small. His aim, however, had been to be victorious, not to win money. He divided the one thousand pounds that remained between Passepartout and the unfortunate Fix, against whom he held no grudge. He deducted, however, from Passepartout’s share the cost of the gas that had burned in his room for nineteen hundred and twenty hours, for the sake of regularity.
That evening, Mr. Fogg, as tranquil and phlegmatic as ever, said to Aouda: “Is our marriage still agreeable to you?”
“Mr. Fogg,” she replied, “it is for me to ask that question. You were ruined, but now you are rich again.”
“Pardon me, madam; my fortune belongs to you. If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson’s, I should not have been told of my error, and—”
“Dear Mr. Fogg!” said the young woman.
“Dear Aouda!” replied Phileas Fogg.

It need hardly be said that the marriage took place forty-eight hours later, and that Passepartout, glowing and dazzling, gave the bride away. Had he not saved her, and was he not entitled to this honour?
The next day, as soon as it was light, Passepartout rapped vigorously at his master’s door. Mr. Fogg opened it, and asked, “What’s the matter, Passepartout?”
“What is it, sir? Why, I’ve just this instant found out—”
“What?”
“That we might have made the tour of the world in only seventy-eight days.”
“No doubt,” replied Mr. Fogg, “by not crossing India. But if I had not crossed India, I should not have saved Aouda; she would not have been my wife, and—”
Mr. Fogg quietly shut the door.

Phileas Fogg had won his wager, and had made his journey around the world in eighty days. To do this he had used every means of conveyance—steamers, railways, carriages, yachts, trading-vessels, sledges, elephants. The eccentric gentleman had throughout displayed all his marvellous qualities of coolness and exactitude. But what then? What had he really gained by all this trouble? What had he brought back from this long and weary journey?
Nothing, say you? Perhaps so; nothing but a charming woman who, strange as it may seem, made him the happiest of men!
Truly, would you not, for less than that, make the tour around the world?
